title: 8  Exercise 2.5 — One split is not an estimate
section: 8.3 The pipeline from Exercise 2.4, rebuilt
text:
8.3 The pipeline from Exercise 2.4, rebuilt
The same regression, the same preprocessing, the same seed: predict body mass index from skin-fold thickness, blood pressure, age and number of pregnancies, with the imputation and scaling fitted inside the workflow so they can only see the training rows.

RPython



library(readr); library(dplyr); library(tidymodels)
tidymodels_prefer()

diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
dia <- diabetes |>
  mutate(across(c(glucose, pressure, triceps, insulin, mass), ~ na_if(.x, 0))) |>
  filter(!is.na(mass)) |>
  select(mass, triceps, pressure, age, pregnant, glucose)

set.seed(42)
split <- initial_split(dia, prop = 0.8)
train <- training(split); test <- testing(split)

rec <- recipe(mass ~ triceps + pressure + age + pregnant, data = train) |>
  step_impute_mean(all_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_predictors())
wf <- workflow() |> add_recipe(rec) |> add_model(linear_reg() |> set_engine("lm"))

mae_baseline <- mean(abs(test$mass - mean(train$mass)))
mae_once <- collect_metrics(last_fit(wf, split = split, metrics = metric_set(mae)))$.estimate
c(baseline = mae_baseline, one_split = mae_once)

#>  baseline one_split 
#>  5.556983  4.457562





import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, KFold, cross_val_score
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer

diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
dia = diabetes.copy()
impossible = ["glucose", "pressure", "triceps", "insulin", "mass"]
dia[impossible] = dia[impossible].replace(0, np.nan)
dia = dia.dropna(subset=["mass"])[
    ["mass", "triceps", "pressure", "age", "pregnant", "glucose"]]
preds = ["triceps", "pressure", "age", "pregnant"]

def build_pipeline():
    numeric = Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="mean")),
                        ("scale", StandardScaler())])
    return Pipeline([("prep", ColumnTransformer([("num", numeric, preds)])),
                     ("model", LinearRegression())])

train, test = train_test_split(dia, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)

mae_baseline = np.abs(test["mass"] - train["mass"].mean()).mean()
pipe = build_pipeline().fit(train[preds], train["mass"])
mae_once = mean_absolute_error(test["mass"], pipe.predict(test[preds]))
print(mae_baseline, mae_once)

#> 5.865293188895224 4.924484517271224





One number each: 4.46 BMI units in R against a baseline of 5.56, and 4.92 against 5.87 in Python. These are the numbers Chapter 7 reported, and the question this exercise asks is what they are estimates of.
The pipeline is wrapped in a function in Python, and in a workflow in R, for a reason that matters below: both have to be refitted from scratch many times, and a fitted object carried over from one split to the next has already seen the rows the next split is about to hold out.

title: 8  Exercise 2.5 — One split is not an estimate
section: 8.4 Task 1 — Fifty splits of the same data
text:
8.4 Task 1 — Fifty splits of the same data
Nothing about the data, the pipeline or the preprocessing changes. Only the random number that decides which 151 rows are held out. Repeat the whole pipeline 50 times, collect the 50 test MAEs, and report the lowest, the highest and the standard deviation.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")

one_split_mae <- function(seed) {
  set.seed(______)
  sp <- initial_split(dia, prop = 0.8)
  collect_metrics(last_fit(wf, split = sp, metrics = metric_set(mae)))$.estimate
}

maes <- vapply(1:50, one_split_mae, numeric(1))
c(lowest = min(maes), highest = max(maes), spread = max(maes) - min(maes),
  mean = mean(maes), sd = ______)
check_metric_range(sd(maes), 0.1, 0.5, "standard deviation of the 50 MAEs")







TipStuck?





vapply() applies a function to each element of a vector and returns a vector of a declared type; the function it is given here takes one seed and returns one MAE. last_fit() re-estimates every recipe step on the training half of whichever split it is handed, so the workflow built above can be reused unchanged. The spread of a sample is sd().






# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *

def one_split_mae(seed):
    tr, te = train_test_split(dia, test_size=0.2, random_state=______)
    p = build_pipeline().fit(tr[preds], tr["mass"])
    return mean_absolute_error(te["mass"], p.predict(te[preds]))

maes = np.array([one_split_mae(s) for s in range(1, 51)])
print(f"lowest {maes.min():.3f} highest {maes.max():.3f} "
      f"spread {np.ptp(maes):.3f} mean {maes.mean():.3f} "
      f"sd {______:.3f}")
check_metric_range(maes.std(ddof=1), 0.1, 0.5, "standard deviation of the 50 MAEs")







TipStuck?





build_pipeline() returns a new unfitted pipeline each time it is called, which is what the loop needs. For the spread, np.ndarray has a .std() method, and its ddof= argument decides whether you get the population or the sample standard deviation; the sample one is what you want here.






The fifty numbers run from 4.01 to 5.20 in R and from 4.13 to 5.26 in Python: a spread of about 1.1 to 1.2 BMI units, produced by nothing but the choice of seed. The standard deviation is 0.28 in R and 0.21 in Python.
Now put that next to the result of Chapter 7. The difference between the honest pipeline and the worst leak measured there was about half a BMI unit. The difference between two equally honest analysts who each ran this pipeline once, with different seeds, can be twice that. Every conclusion Day 2 drew by comparing pipelines on one split was drawn against a ruler with that much play in it.
Worse, you cannot tell from one run which draw you got. Seed 42 is in the fifty. In R its MAE is the nineteenth smallest of the fifty and sits 0.13 below their mean; in Python the same number 42 gives the forty-eighth of fifty, 0.38 above the mean and among the worst draws available. Two students, two languages, the same code: one of them would have reported a pipeline that looks slightly better than it is, the other one that looks about a third of a BMI unit worse.

title: 8  Exercise 2.5 — One split is not an estimate
section: 8.5 Task 2 — Ten folds, one estimate, one standard error
text:
8.5 Task 2 — Ten folds, one estimate, one standard error
Fifty repeats of an 80/20 split is not the usual way to do this, because the fifty test sets overlap heavily and each one wastes a fifth of the data at every repeat. Cross-validation partitions the rows instead: cut the training rows into ten parts, fit on nine, score on the one left out, ten times, so that every training row is scored exactly once and every score comes from a model that did not see it.
Note which rows are being cut. The test set is not in this at all — it stays closed.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
set.seed(42)
folds <- vfold_cv(______, v = 10)        # which rows go into the folds?
folds

cv_res <- fit_resamples(wf, resamples = ______, metrics = metric_set(mae))
collect_metrics(cv_res)

cv_mean <- collect_metrics(cv_res)$mean
cv_se   <- collect_metrics(cv_res)$std_err
per_fold <- collect_metrics(cv_res, summarize = FALSE)$.estimate
c(folds_lowest = min(per_fold), folds_highest = max(per_fold))
check_beats_baseline(cv_mean, mae_baseline)







TipStuck?





vfold_cv() takes a data frame; the whole argument of this task is which frame it must not be given. fit_resamples() takes the same workflow you already built and the resamples object, and refits the recipe inside every fold. collect_metrics(..., summarize = FALSE) returns one row per fold rather than the average.






# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
folds = KFold(n_splits=______, shuffle=True, random_state=42)

fold_mae = -cross_val_score(build_pipeline(), ______[preds], ______["mass"],
                            cv=folds, scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error")
cv_mean = fold_mae.mean()
cv_se   = fold_mae.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(10)
print(np.round(fold_mae, 3))
print(f"mean {cv_mean:.3f}, standard error {cv_se:.3f}, "
      f"folds {fold_mae.min():.3f} to {fold_mae.max():.3f}")
check_beats_baseline(cv_mean, mae_baseline)







TipStuck?





cross_val_score clones the estimator and refits it inside every fold, which is why it is handed build_pipeline() and not the pipe already fitted above. Scikit-learn’s scorers are oriented so that higher is better, hence the minus sign in front of a mean absolute error. The two blanks after it are the same frame, and it is not dia.






The ten-fold mean is 4.56 in R and 4.47 in Python, with a standard error of 0.15 and 0.17. Two things in that output are worth more than the mean.
First, the individual folds are more variable than the fifty splits were: 3.91 to 5.35 in R, 3.72 to 5.36 in Python. That is not a contradiction. Each fold scores about 60 rows where each split scored 151, so a single fold is a noisier measurement than a single split; what cross-validation gives you is not a quieter measurement but ten of them, averaged.
Second, count the fits. Fifty repeated splits cost fifty fits and returned a mean whose standard error is 0.03 to 0.04. Ten folds cost ten fits and returned a mean whose standard error is 0.15 to 0.17 — against a standard deviation of 0.21 to 0.28 for the single number you would otherwise have reported. Ten fits therefore bought a reduction in uncertainty of between a fifth and a half, not the factor of three that dividing by \(\sqrt{10}\) might have suggested, because the ten training sets overlap in nine tenths of their rows and the ten scores are not independent. On 604 rows and a linear model all of this is a second or two; on a model that takes an hour to fit, the choice between 10 folds, 5 folds and one split is a budget decision, and it is the usual reason published models are evaluated on one split.

title: 8  Exercise 2.5 — One split is not an estimate
section: 8.6 The result that should bother you
text:
8.6 The result that should bother you
Everything above refits the preprocessing inside every fold, because the workflow and the Pipeline leave no other option. The common failure in practice is to do one preprocessing step by hand first — on the whole training set, once, because it is tidier — and then cross-validate what comes out. This is Chapter 7’s mistake moved inside the resampling loop, and the loop hides it.
Here is that mistake with a step that can carry real information: choosing which predictors to keep. Two hundred columns of pure random numbers are added to the training rows, the ten most correlated with BMI are selected, and the selected set is cross-validated. Then the same thing, with the selection repeated inside each fold.

RPython



set.seed(7)
noise <- as.data.frame(matrix(rnorm(nrow(train) * 200), nrow(train), 200))
names(noise) <- paste0("noise", 1:200)
train_noise <- bind_cols(train["mass"], noise)
noise_cols  <- names(noise)

top_k <- function(d, k = 10) {
  r <- vapply(noise_cols, function(v) abs(cor(d[[v]], d$mass)), numeric(1))
  names(sort(r, decreasing = TRUE))[1:k]
}
chosen_once <- top_k(train_noise)        # chosen ONCE, on all the training rows

set.seed(99)
noise_folds <- vfold_cv(train_noise, v = 10)
fold_score <- function(sp, choose) {
  fit_rows <- analysis(sp); score_rows <- assessment(sp)
  m <- lm(reformulate(choose(fit_rows), "mass"), data = fit_rows)
  mean(abs(score_rows$mass - predict(m, score_rows)))
}

cv_outside <- mean(vapply(noise_folds$splits,
                          function(sp) fold_score(sp, function(d) chosen_once), numeric(1)))
cv_inside  <- mean(vapply(noise_folds$splits,
                          function(sp) fold_score(sp, top_k), numeric(1)))
cv_nothing <- mean(vapply(noise_folds$splits, function(sp)
  mean(abs(assessment(sp)$mass - mean(analysis(sp)$mass))), numeric(1)))

c(selected_outside = cv_outside, selected_inside = cv_inside,
  predict_the_mean = cv_nothing)

#> selected_outside  selected_inside predict_the_mean 
#>         5.390850         5.726338         5.469583



source("checks/checks.R")
check_beats_baseline(cv_outside, cv_nothing)

#> [ok]  the model beats the predict-the-mean baseline  (model 5.39 vs baseline 5.47 (99% of the baseline error))

check_beats_baseline(cv_inside,  cv_nothing)

#> [fix] the model beats the predict-the-mean baseline  (model 5.73 vs baseline 5.47 (105% of the baseline error))
#>        hint: a model that does not beat the baseline has learnt nothing worth having





from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_regression
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
noise = pd.DataFrame(rng.normal(size=(len(train), 200)),
                     columns=[f"noise{i}" for i in range(1, 201)],
                     index=train.index)
y = train["mass"]
noise_folds = KFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=99)

chosen_once = SelectKBest(f_regression, k=10).fit(noise, y)   # ONCE, on all of it
cv_outside = -cross_val_score(LinearRegression(),
                              noise.loc[:, chosen_once.get_support()], y,
                              cv=noise_folds,
                              scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error").mean()

cv_inside = -cross_val_score(Pipeline([("select", SelectKBest(f_regression, k=10)),
                                       ("model", LinearRegression())]),
                             noise, y, cv=noise_folds,
                             scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error").mean()

cv_nothing = -cross_val_score(DummyRegressor(strategy="mean"), noise, y,
                              cv=noise_folds,
                              scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error").mean()

print(cv_outside, cv_inside, cv_nothing)

#> 5.25927159961368 5.748932066996416 5.371907196561035



import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
check_beats_baseline(cv_outside, cv_nothing)

#> [ok]  the model beats the predict-the-mean baseline  (model 5.26 vs baseline 5.37 (98% of the baseline error))

check_beats_baseline(cv_inside,  cv_nothing)

#> [fix] the model beats the predict-the-mean baseline  (model 5.75 vs baseline 5.37 (107% of the baseline error))
#>        hint: a model that does not beat the baseline has learnt nothing worth having





There is no signal in those 200 columns. They are random numbers, and no estimate of a model built from them should beat predicting the mean. Selected outside the loop, the cross-validated MAE is 5.39 in R and 5.26 in Python against a do-nothing 5.47 and 5.37: it beats the baseline, and check_beats_baseline() prints [ok]. Selected inside the loop, the same ten folds, the same rule, the same random numbers, give 5.73 and 5.75 — worse than the baseline, which is the truth.

The selection step read the outcome. It was allowed to read it on all 604 training rows, including the 60 that each fold then held out for scoring.
So every fold’s held-out rows had already voted on which ten columns the model would use. The ten fits inside the loop are honest; the thing being evaluated is not a procedure applied to 544 rows, it is a procedure that already saw 604.
Cross-validation cannot detect this, because it only controls what happens after it is handed the data. A fitted step performed before the loop is invisible to it — the loop faithfully cross-validates a model that has already been given the answers.

The same mistake made with the imputation and scaling of Chapter 7 costs almost nothing, as Stretch 1 asks you to confirm. The difference is not how careless the analyst was. It is the same distinction Chapter 7 drew: a mean carries almost no row-specific information, and a choice made among 200 candidates by looking at the outcome carries a great deal.
Note also what the self-check did. check_beats_baseline() printed [ok] for a pipeline built on random numbers. A check is only as good as the assumption written into it, and no check in this booklet can see what you did to the data before you called it.

8.7 Task 3 — Three kinds of row
Assemble the three estimates of the same pipeline into one table, then write the sentence it supports. Keep the model_fits column: the three numbers are not equally cheap, and the table is useless without that.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
tibble(
  estimate = c("one split (Exercise 2.4)", "50 repeated splits",
               "10-fold on the training rows"),
  value = c(mae_once, mean(maes), ______),
  uncertainty = c(NA, sd(maes), cv_se),
  model_fits = c(1, ______, 10)
)




# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
pd.DataFrame({
    "estimate": ["one split (Exercise 2.4)", "50 repeated splits",
                 "10-fold on the training rows"],
    "value": [mae_once, maes.mean(), ______],
    "uncertainty": [np.nan, maes.std(ddof=1), cv_se],
    "model_fits": [1, ______, 10],
}).round(3)




Then answer in writing, in one sentence each: which rows were fitted, which rows chose something, and which rows were spent in each of the three lines of your table. The middle role is empty in all three, because nothing has been chosen yet — Chapter 19 is where it fills up, and it is the reason the folds exist at all.
That distinction is what the rest of the booklet runs on, and it is worth writing out once:








Role
Which rows
How often they can be used




Fitted
the analysis part of a fold, or the training set for the final model
as often as you like


Chose a setting
the assessment part of each fold
as often as you like, but a score computed on them is no longer held out


Spent
the test set
once, at the very end, and never again



A row may do the first two jobs in different folds; that is what resampling is. A row that does the third must never have done either of the others. Measure your own three estimates against that. The worked example opened the test set once. Task 1 opened fifty different test sets, which is defensible only because its purpose was to measure the spread and not to report a performance — the mean of those fifty is not a held-out number, because every row was fitted in some repeats and scored in others. Task 2 is the only one of the three that left the test rows closed.

Can: that this pipeline predicts BMI to within about 4.5 units on held-out rows, with a standard error of about 0.15 — and that you can produce that second half of the sentence, in either language, with one resampling object and ten fits, rather than reporting a single split that these data would have put anywhere between 4.0 and 5.3.

title: 9  Exercise 3.1 — Supervised learning
section: 9.2 Why this, here
text:
9.2 Why this, here
In Chapter 2 you fitted a model with one call and read a score off the test set. The fitting itself was a black box: fit() went in, coefficients came out. Today we open it. This exercise sets up the pieces — data, algorithm, fitted parameters, prediction — so that Chapter 10 can ask what “best fit” means and Chapter 11 can ask how the best fit is found.

title: 9  Exercise 3.1 — Supervised learning
section: 9.3 The data we fit to
text:
9.3 The data we fit to
Today’s outcome is a blood glucose measurement and the single predictor is age. The question behind it: does knowing a patient’s age tell you anything useful about their glucose? The answer today is more interesting than you might expect.
data/diabetes.csv is the module’s case study: 768 adults screened for type 2 diabetes, eight measurements from a single visit and a pos/neg outcome. It carries the defect you met on Day 2 — five rows record a glucose of 0, which is not a measurement — so we drop those rows and keep the first 80 of what is left, small enough to see every point on a scatter plot.

RPython



library(readr); library(dplyr); library(ggplot2)

diab <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
glu  <- diab |> filter(glucose > 0) |> slice(1:80) |> select(age, glucose)

nrow(glu)

#> [1] 80

head(glu)

#> # A tibble: 6 × 2
#>     age glucose
#>   <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1    28     194
#> 2    44     129
#> 3    26     132
#> 4    39     184
#> 5    22     108
#> 6    58     117





import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

diab = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
glu = (diab.loc[diab["glucose"] > 0, ["age", "glucose"]]
           .head(80)
           .reset_index(drop=True))

len(glu), glu.head()

#> (80,    age  glucose
#> 0   28      194
#> 1   44      129
#> 2   26      132
#> 3   39      184
#> 4   22      108)






RPython



ggplot(glu, aes(x = age, y = glucose)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Age in years (the feature)",
       y = "Glucose, mg/dL (the label)")











import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(glu["age"], glu["glucose"], alpha=0.7)
ax.set_xlabel("Age in years (the feature)")
ax.set_ylabel("Glucose, mg/dL (the label)")
plt.show()











Look at the scatter before you fit anything, and write down what slope you expect. You will be asked for it again at the end.

title: 9  Exercise 3.1 — Supervised learning
section: 9.4 The three things that make a prediction
text:
9.4 The three things that make a prediction









What it is
In the code below




The learning algorithm
a procedure for turning data into parameters
linear_reg(), LinearRegression()


The fitted model
the parameters it produced, and nothing else
\(\hat\beta_0 = 110.30\), \(\hat\beta_1 = 0.289\)


The dataset
what the algorithm was allowed to see
the 80 rows in glu



The algorithm is chosen by you, the parameters are chosen by the data, and the prediction is a consequence of both. Students conflate the first two constantly: “linear regression predicted 123” is wrong, because linear regression predicts nothing until it has been shown a dataset.
In machine learning notation the model is written
\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1\]
where \(y\) is the label (glucose), \(x_1\) the feature (age), \(\beta_0\) the intercept — often called the bias — and \(\beta_1\) the weight on the feature, which is the slope. Both are parameters: numbers the fitting procedure returns.

title: 9  Exercise 3.1 — Supervised learning
section: 9.5 Fitting, in both languages
text:
9.5 Fitting, in both languages

RPython



library(parsnip)

lm_model <- linear_reg() |> set_engine("lm") |> set_mode("regression")
ls_fit   <- lm_model |> fit(glucose ~ age, data = glu)

coef(extract_fit_engine(ls_fit))

#> (Intercept)         age 
#> 110.2979509   0.2886749





from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

X = glu[["age"]]      # 2-D: a frame, not a series
y = glu["glucose"]    # 1-D
lin_reg = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)

lin_reg.intercept_, lin_reg.coef_[0]

#> (np.float64(110.2979509174209), np.float64(0.28867490665401274))





The two agree to every decimal worth printing, because both solve the same least-squares problem on the same 80 rows. Chapter 12 shows you the algebra they are solving and verifies it by hand.






Warningcoef() does not work on a parsnip fit



coef(ls_fit) returns NULL — silently, with no error. A model_fit object wraps the engine’s fit rather than being one, so you have to reach inside with extract_fit_engine() first. Passing the NULL to geom_abline() then fails some distance from the line that caused it, which is the most annoying class of bug there is.


So the fitted model is
\[\widehat{\text{glucose}} = 110.30 + 0.289 \times \text{age}\]
and that is the entire deliverable of the fitting step. Two numbers.

title: 9  Exercise 3.1 — Supervised learning
section: 9.6 Predicting, inside and outside the data
text:
9.6 Predicting, inside and outside the data

RPython



new_patients <- data.frame(age = c(45, 10))
predict(ls_fit, new_data = new_patients)

#> # A tibble: 2 × 1
#>   .pred
#>   <dbl>
#> 1  123.
#> 2  113.





lin_reg.predict(pd.DataFrame({"age": [45, 10]}))

#> array([123.28832172, 113.18469998])





A 45-year-old gets a predicted glucose of about 123.3. So does a 10-year-old, at about 113.2 — even though the youngest patient in the data is 21, and these are adults with no children among them. The model is an infinite line. It will return a number for an age of 200, or of −40, and nothing in the code will object.






NoteExtrapolation is a modelling decision, not a software error



The line is fitted on ages 21 to 81. Using it at 10 asserts that the same relationship holds in children, which nothing in these data supports. Every model will happily extrapolate; the restraint has to come from you. Note also what the model does not give you: any sense of how confident it is. That is a statistical question and this is a prediction course.

9.8 Task 2 — Make the line earn its place
A fitted line is only worth having if it beats a predictor that does no learning. Compute the mean squared error of the line on these 80 rows, and the mean squared error of predicting the mean glucose for everybody.
Both numbers are computed on the rows the model was fitted to, which Chapter 2 told you is not evidence of anything. Today that is deliberate: this exercise is about what fitting does, not about how well it generalises. Read every number on this page as in-sample.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")

The check prints the line’s error as a percentage of the baseline’s. Write the percentage down before you read the next section.

title: 9  Exercise 3.1 — Supervised learning
section: 9.9 The result that should bother you
text:
9.9 The result that should bother you
The line’s in-sample mean squared error is 847.5. The mean squared error of ignoring age entirely and predicting 119.9 for everyone is 863.2. Fitting removed 1.8% of the squared error.
Now destroy the relationship on purpose and fit again. Shuffling the age column breaks any link between a patient’s age and their glucose while leaving both distributions exactly as they were.

RPython



set.seed(42)
glu_shuffled <- glu |> mutate(age = sample(age))

fit_shuffled  <- lm_model |> fit(glucose ~ age, data = glu_shuffled)
pred_shuffled <- predict(fit_shuffled, new_data = glu_shuffled)$.pred

coef(extract_fit_engine(fit_shuffled))

#> (Intercept)         age 
#> 128.7674274  -0.2665893

mean((glu_shuffled$glucose - pred_shuffled)^2)

#> [1] 849.8275





rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
glu_shuffled = glu.assign(age=rng.permutation(glu["age"].values))

fit_shuffled = LinearRegression().fit(glu_shuffled[["age"]], glu_shuffled["glucose"])
mse_shuffled = np.mean((glu_shuffled["glucose"]
                        - fit_shuffled.predict(glu_shuffled[["age"]]))**2)

fit_shuffled.intercept_, fit_shuffled.coef_[0], mse_shuffled

#> (np.float64(116.54068704973496), np.float64(0.10099400075956573), np.float64(861.2722501680768))





Three steps of reasoning.

Shuffled age cannot predict glucose. Any apparent fit is coincidence, and its error is what “no relationship at all” looks like in these units.
The shuffled fit’s error is around 850 in R and around 861 in Python — the two seeds shuffle differently — against 847.5 for the real age column and 863.2 for the baseline. The real predictor buys you almost nothing that a deliberately broken one does not.
The algebra in Chapter 12 is exact, the fit is genuinely the best straight line there is, and the model is still not worth deploying. A minimum is not the same thing as a small number.

Keep this: the entire day is about finding the best line, and the best line here is nearly useless. Being able to hold both of those at once is the point.

title: 9  Exercise 3.1 — Supervised learning
section: 9.10 Task 3 — Change the algorithm, keep everything else
text:
9.10 Task 3 — Change the algorithm, keep everything else
A decision tree is a different learning algorithm applied to the identical dataset and the identical question. You meet trees properly in Chapter 19; for now, swap one line and look at the shape of what comes out.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
library(rpart); library(rpart.plot)

dt_model <- decision_tree(mode = "regression") |> set_engine("______")
dt_fit   <- dt_model |> fit(glucose ~ age, data = glu)

rpart.plot(extract_fit_engine(dt_fit), roundint = FALSE)







TipStuck?





The engine is the package that does the work, exactly as "lm" was for linear_reg(). For trees in R it is the recursive-partitioning package, and the string is its name.






# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor, export_text

tree_reg = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, min_samples_leaf=5).fit(______, ______)
print(export_text(tree_reg, feature_names=["age"]))







TipStuck?





The tree takes the same two arguments the linear model took, in the same order.






Now plot both models’ predictions over the data. The line is a line; the tree is a staircase, constant within each age band it chose.

RPython



dt_fit_shown <- decision_tree(mode = "regression") |> set_engine("rpart") |>
  fit(glucose ~ age, data = glu)

glu_pred <- glu |>
  mutate(pred_tree = predict(dt_fit_shown, new_data = glu)$.pred,
         pred_line = predict(ls_fit,       new_data = glu)$.pred)

ggplot(glu_pred, aes(x = age)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = glucose), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_step(aes(y = pred_tree), colour = "darkred", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = pred_line), colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Glucose (mg/dL)")











from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
tree_shown = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, min_samples_leaf=5).fit(X, y)

grid = pd.DataFrame({"age": np.linspace(glu["age"].min(), glu["age"].max(), 400)})
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(glu["age"], glu["glucose"], alpha=0.5)
ax.plot(grid["age"], tree_shown.predict(grid), color="darkred")
ax.plot(grid["age"], lin_reg.predict(grid), color="steelblue")
ax.set_xlabel("Age (years)"); ax.set_ylabel("Glucose (mg/dL)")
plt.show()











The tree’s in-sample mean squared error is lower than the line’s: 685.7 in R with rpart’s default pruning, 677.9 in Python with a depth of 3. Both are well below the line’s 847.5. The tree is not better. It has more parameters — one mean per leaf rather than two numbers for the whole dataset — and more parameters always fit the rows you fitted them to more closely. Chapter 19 is where that argument gets settled.






NoteThe two trees are not the same tree



rpart and scikit-learn choose splits the same way but stop differently: rpart prunes using a complexity parameter and cross-validation, scikit-learn stops when you tell it to. Ours end up with six leaves and seven respectively. Unlike the linear coefficients, which agreed to the decimal, the trees are a genuine difference between the two libraries’ defaults, and you should expect to have to state tree-stopping rules explicitly whenever you report one.

title: 9  Exercise 3.1 — Supervised learning
section: 9.14 What you can and cannot now claim
text:
9.14 What you can and cannot now claim
Can: that you can fit, read and apply a two-parameter model in both languages, swap the learning algorithm without touching anything else, and state what the dataset contributed to the result.
Cannot: that this line is the best one. We never defined “best” — we used whatever lm() optimises, which happens to be squared error. That choice does real work, and it is Chapter 10.

title: 10  Exercise 3.2 — Loss functions
text: 10.1 Objectives

title: 10  Exercise 3.2 — Loss functions
text:
Compute a residual, a sum of squared residuals, a mean squared error and a mean absolute error from a set of predictions, in both languages, without looking up a formula.

title: 10  Exercise 3.2 — Loss functions
section: 10.2 Why this, here
text:
10.2 Why this, here
Chapter 9 fitted a line and called it the best fit, without ever saying best at what. This exercise supplies the missing definition. A loss function scores a candidate line against the data; the fitting procedure returns the line with the lowest score. Change the score and you change the line — and then Chapter 11 asks how the lowest score is found at all.

title: 10  Exercise 3.2 — Loss functions
section: 10.4 One point, one residual
text:
10.4 One point, one residual
A residual is what the model got wrong for one patient:
\[r_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i\]
Take a line nobody fitted — \(\widehat{\text{glucose}} = 120 + 0.5 \times
\text{age}\), invented by hand — and find the patient it serves worst.

RPython



glu <- glu |> mutate(pred_guess = 120 + 0.5 * age,
                     resid_guess = glucose - pred_guess)

worst <- glu |> slice_max(abs(resid_guess), n = 1)
worst

#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>     age glucose pred_guess resid_guess
#>   <dbl>   <dbl>      <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1    58      72        149         -77





glu["pred_guess"] = 120 + 0.5 * glu["age"]
glu["resid_guess"] = glu["glucose"] - glu["pred_guess"]

worst = glu.loc[[glu["resid_guess"].abs().idxmax()]]
worst

#>     age  glucose  pred_guess  resid_guess
#> 41   58       72       149.0        -77.0





That patient is 58, their measured glucose is 72, the hand-drawn line predicts 149, and the residual is −77 mg/dL — an error larger than the measurement itself.

RPython



ggplot(glu, aes(x = age, y = glucose)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 120, slope = 0.5, colour = "darkorange", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = age, yend = pred_guess), colour = "red", alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Glucose (mg/dL)")











import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(glu["age"], glu["glucose"], alpha=0.6)
ax.vlines(glu["age"], glu["pred_guess"], glu["glucose"], color="red", alpha=0.3)
ax.plot(glu["age"], glu["pred_guess"], color="darkorange")
ax.set_xlabel("Age (years)"); ax.set_ylabel("Glucose (mg/dL)")
plt.show()











The red segments are the residuals. A loss function is a rule for turning all 80 of them into one number.

title: 10  Exercise 3.2 — Loss functions
section: 10.5 Four ways to add up 80 mistakes
text:
10.5 Four ways to add up 80 mistakes
Residuals are positive and negative, so adding them cancels most of the error away. Two repairs are in common use, and they are not equivalent.
\[\text{SSR} = \sum_{i=1}^{m} r_i^2 \qquad
\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} r_i^2 \qquad
\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} \left| r_i \right|\]
Squaring is the L2 loss; taking the absolute value is the L1 loss. The mean squared error is the sum of squared residuals divided by the number of rows, so it does not grow simply because the dataset is larger. The root of the MSE — RMSE — is back in the outcome’s units and is easier to quote.

RPython



loss_table <- function(residuals) {
  m <- length(residuals)              # the number of residuals passed in,
  ssr <- sum(residuals^2)             # not the size of some data frame
  c(SSR = ssr, MSE = ssr / m, RMSE = sqrt(ssr / m),
    MAE = mean(abs(residuals)))
}

round(loss_table(glu$resid_guess), 3)

#>       SSR       MSE      RMSE       MAE 
#> 90868.250  1135.853    33.702    28.656





def loss_table(residuals):
    residuals = np.asarray(residuals)
    m = len(residuals)
    ssr = np.sum(residuals**2)
    return {"SSR": ssr, "MSE": ssr / m, "RMSE": np.sqrt(ssr / m),
            "MAE": np.mean(np.abs(residuals))}

{k: round(v, 3) for k, v in loss_table(glu["resid_guess"]).items()}

#> {'SSR': np.float64(90868.25), 'MSE': np.float64(1135.853), 'RMSE': np.float64(33.702), 'MAE': np.float64(28.656)}





The hand-drawn line scores SSR 90868, MSE 1135.9, RMSE 33.7 and MAE 28.7. RMSE and MAE are both in mg/dL and the RMSE is the larger of the two, which is not an accident: squaring weights the worst patients more heavily, so any summary built from squares sits above the plain average error whenever the residuals are unequal.

10.6 Task 1 — Score the fitted line against the hand-drawn one
Fit the least-squares line, compute its residuals, and put them through loss_table().

RPython

source("checks/checks.R")
fit_ols   <- lm(glucose ~ age, data = glu)
resid_ols <- ______                     # the residuals of the fitted line
losses    <- loss_table(resid_ols)
round(losses, 3)
check_metric_range(losses[["MAE"]], 20, 25, "MAE of the fitted line")







TipStuck?





lm() keeps the residuals for you; resid() is the accessor. Subtracting the predictions from the outcome by hand gives the same vector, and it is worth doing once to satisfy yourself of that.






# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.

from checks import *
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

X, y = glu[["age"]], glu["glucose"]
fit_ols   = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
resid_ols = ______                      # the residuals of the fitted line

print({k: round(v, 3) for k, v in losses.items()})
check_metric_range(losses["MAE"], 20, 25, "MAE of the fitted line")




The fitted line scores MSE 847.5 against the hand-drawn line’s 1135.9, and MAE 22.3 against 28.7. It wins on both. That is reassuring but not guaranteed: the fitted line is the best line for squared error, and nothing in the procedure promises it also has the lowest absolute error. Hold that thought.

title: 10  Exercise 3.2 — Loss functions
section: 10.7 Task 2 — Contaminate three readings
text:
10.7 Task 2 — Contaminate three readings
Three glucose values are recorded three times too large — a plausible unit or transcription error. Multiply rows 1, 3 and 5 by three, refit, and compare.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
glu_bad <- glu
glu_bad$glucose[c(1, 3, 5)] <- glu_bad$glucose[c(1, 3, 5)] * ______

fit_bad <- lm(glucose ~ age, data = ______)
rbind(clean = coef(fit_ols), contaminated = coef(fit_bad))




# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
glu_bad = glu.copy()
glu_bad.loc[[0, 2, 4], "glucose"] = glu_bad.loc[[0, 2, 4], "glucose"] * ______

fit_bad = LinearRegression().fit(glu_bad[["age"]], ______)
{"clean": (fit_ols.intercept_, fit_ols.coef_[0]),
 "contaminated": (fit_bad.intercept_, fit_bad.coef_[0])}







TipStuck?





R counts rows from 1 and pandas from 0, so rows 1, 3 and 5 are [0, 2, 4] in Python. This is the one indexing difference that silently changes a result rather than raising an error.






Three rows out of eighty — under four per cent of the data — moved the intercept from 110.3 to 135.3 and turned the slope from +0.289 to −0.136. The fitted line now says glucose falls with age. Nothing warned you; the fit succeeded, as it always does.

title: 10  Exercise 3.2 — Loss functions
section: 10.8 The result that should bother you
text:
10.8 The result that should bother you
The obvious reading is that outliers break regression. They do not. They break this loss.
Fit the same straight line by minimising mean absolute error instead of mean squared error. There is no closed form, so hand the loss to a general-purpose optimiser.

RPython



fit_lad <- function(data) {
  loss <- function(p) mean(abs(data$glucose - (p[1] + p[2] * data$age)))
  optim(c(mean(data$glucose), 0), loss, method = "Nelder-Mead",
        control = list(maxit = 5000, reltol = 1e-12))$par
}

glu_bad <- glu
glu_bad$glucose[c(1, 3, 5)] <- glu_bad$glucose[c(1, 3, 5)] * 3

rbind(clean = fit_lad(glu), contaminated = fit_lad(glu_bad))

#>                 [,1]   [,2]
#> clean        101.875 0.4375
#> contaminated 101.875 0.4375





from scipy.optimize import minimize

def fit_lad(data):
    loss = lambda p: np.mean(np.abs(data["glucose"] - (p[0] + p[1] * data["age"])))
    return minimize(loss, [data["glucose"].mean(), 0.0], method="Nelder-Mead",
                    options={"maxiter": 5000, "fatol": 1e-12, "xatol": 1e-10}).x

glu_bad = glu.copy()
glu_bad.loc[[0, 2, 4], "glucose"] = glu_bad.loc[[0, 2, 4], "glucose"] * 3

{"clean": fit_lad(glu), "contaminated": fit_lad(glu_bad)}

#> {'clean': array([101.875 ,   0.4375]), 'contaminated': array([101.875 ,   0.4375])}





Three steps of reasoning.

The least-absolute-error line is intercept 101.9, slope 0.4375 on the clean data — and intercept 101.9, slope 0.4375 on the contaminated data. To four decimal places, the contamination did not move it at all. Both languages agree, having started from the same guess and minimised the same function.
Squaring is the mechanism. Tripling a glucose of 194 to 582 multiplies its contribution to the MSE by roughly the square of how far out it now is, so the line is dragged towards it; under absolute error that patient contributes its distance and no more, and three votes out of eighty do not carry.
So “the best fit line” is not a property of the data. It is a property of the data and the loss you chose, and the choice was made for you by whoever wrote lm().







NoteWhy squared error anyway



If absolute error is this much more robust, why is every default squared? Two reasons, and only one of them is about statistics. The squared loss is differentiable everywhere, which is what lets Chapter 11 follow a gradient and Chapter 12 solve for the answer in closed form; absolute error has a kink at zero and needs a different class of algorithm. And the mean is the minimiser of squared error while the median minimises absolute error, so the two losses are answering different questions about the outcome, not the same question with different robustness. Convenience, then interpretation — in that order, historically.

title: 10  Exercise 3.2 — Loss functions
section: 10.9 How the loss changes as the line moves
text:
10.9 How the loss changes as the line moves
So far a loss has scored a line someone else supplied. Now treat it as a function of the parameters, which is what fitting actually optimises:
\[\text{MSE}(\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m}
\left( y_i - \left( \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x_i \right) \right)^2\]
Start by hand with the first three patients, aged 28, 44 and 26, with glucose 194, 129 and 132. For \(\hat\beta_0 = 3\) and \(\hat\beta_1 = 5\) the predictions are 143, 223 and 133, so
\[\frac{(194-143)^2 + (129-223)^2 + (132-133)^2}{3}
= \frac{2601 + 8836 + 1}{3} = 3812.67\]

text:

              label = "MSE of (3, 5) on the first three patients")

c(at_3_5 = mse_of(3, 5, glu$age, glu$glucose),
  at_4_7 = mse_of(4, 7, glu$age, glu$glucose))







TipStuck?





The predicted value for one patient is the intercept plus the slope times that patient’s age. Everything else — the subtraction, the square, the mean — is already written.

    return np.mean((y - (______))**2)

{"at_3_5": mse_of(3, 5, glu["age"], glu["glucose"]),

On all 80 rows those two candidates score 7462 and 22991 against the fitted line’s 847.5. Both are terrible, and the first is better than the second, which is all a loss is for: ranking candidates.






WarningWhich number is the intercept



Writing \(\hat\beta_0 = 3\), \(\hat\beta_1 = 5\) and then drawing geom_abline(slope = 3, intercept = 5) plots a different line from the one you scored, and the plot will look convincing. geom_abline() takes slope and intercept by name for exactly this reason. Name both arguments, every time.

title: 10  Exercise 3.2 — Loss functions
section: 10.11 The whole surface at once
text:
10.11 The whole surface at once
Evaluate the MSE over a grid of candidate parameter values — 101 intercepts between 60 and 160, 151 slopes between −1 and 2, 15,251 lines in total — and draw the result. The red point is what lm() returned.

RPython



library(tidyr); library(purrr)

mse_of  <- function(beta0, beta1, x, y) mean((y - (beta0 + beta1 * x))^2)
fit_ols <- lm(glucose ~ age, data = glu)

grid <- expand_grid(b0 = seq(60, 160, by = 1),
                    b1 = seq(-1, 2, by = 0.02)) |>
  mutate(MSE = map2_dbl(b0, b1, ~ mse_of(.x, .y, glu$age, glu$glucose)))

ggplot(grid, aes(x = b0, y = b1)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill = log10(MSE))) +
  geom_contour(aes(z = log10(MSE)), colour = "white", alpha = 0.4, bins = 12) +
  annotate("point", x = coef(fit_ols)[[1]], y = coef(fit_ols)[[2]],
           colour = "red", size = 3) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma") +
  labs(x = expression(hat(beta)[0]), y = expression(hat(beta)[1]),
       fill = "log10(MSE)")











from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
fit_ols = LinearRegression().fit(glu[["age"]], glu["glucose"])

def mse_of(beta0, beta1, x, y):
    return np.mean((y - (beta0 + beta1 * x))**2)

b0_vals = np.arange(60, 160.001, 1.0)
b1_vals = np.arange(-1, 2.0001, 0.02)
B0, B1 = np.meshgrid(b0_vals, b1_vals, indexing="ij")
resid_grid = glu["glucose"].values - (B0[..., None] + B1[..., None] * glu["age"].values)
MSE = (resid_grid**2).mean(axis=-1)       # average over patients, not parameters

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
cs = ax.contourf(B0, B1, np.log10(MSE), levels=20, cmap="magma")
ax.scatter([fit_ols.intercept_], [fit_ols.coef_[0]], color="red", zorder=3)
fig.colorbar(cs, ax=ax, label="log10(MSE)")

#> <matplotlib.colorbar.Colorbar object at 0x306126f10>

ax.set_xlabel(r"$\hat\beta_0$"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$\hat\beta_1$")
plt.show()











Two features of that picture matter for the next exercise. The surface is a bowl: it has one lowest point and no others, which is why least squares has a single answer. And the bowl is a long diagonal trough rather than a round basin, because the intercept and the slope trade off against each other — raise the slope and you can compensate by lowering the intercept. Chapter 11 walks downhill on this exact surface, and the shape of the trough is what makes that harder than it sounds.

10.12 Task 4 — Find the minimum by brute force
Pull the lowest cell out of the grid you just built and compare it with the fitted line.

RPython

source("checks/checks.R")
best <- grid |> slice_min(______, n = 1)
best

check_matches(best$b1, coef(fit_ols)[["age"]], tol = 0.05,
              label = "grid-search slope")







TipStuck?





slice_min() takes the name of the column to minimise, unquoted.






# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *

i, j = np.unravel_index(MSE.______(), MSE.shape)
print(b0_vals[i], b1_vals[j], MSE[i, j])

check_matches(b1_vals[j], fit_ols.coef_[0], tol=0.05, label="grid-search slope")







TipStuck?





You want the position of the smallest value in a 2-D array, which numpy gives you as a flat index; unravel_index is already there to turn it back into a row and a column.






The grid’s best cell is intercept 110, slope 0.30, with an MSE of 847.55 — against lm()’s 110.298, 0.2887 and 847.52. The difference is the spacing of the grid and nothing else.






NoteWhy not just use the grid



Fifteen thousand evaluations to recover two numbers already feels wasteful, and it is: the grid also has to be centred near the answer to find it, which requires knowing the answer. With ten parameters rather than two, a grid of this resolution would need more evaluations than there are atoms in the room. Grid search is a teaching device here, not a method.

text:
10.14 Stretch






NoteStretch 1 — Where does the squared loss put the line



Contaminate a single patient rather than three, and increase the multiplier from 1 to 10 in steps, refitting each time. Plot the fitted slope against the multiplier. The relationship is close to linear, and it has no breakpoint: there is no size of error at which squared loss decides to ignore a point.

title: 10  Exercise 3.2 — Loss functions
section: 10.15 What you can and cannot now claim
text:
10.15 What you can and cannot now claim
Can: that you can compute any of the standard regression losses from residuals, state what each does with a badly mispredicted patient, and demonstrate that the best fit line depends on which loss was chosen.
Cannot: that you can find the minimum of a loss for any model worth fitting. A grid of 15,251 candidates found two parameters approximately. Chapter 11 replaces the grid with a method that uses the slope of the loss itself.

title: 11  Exercise 3.3 — Gradient descent
text: 11.1 Objectives

title: 11  Exercise 3.3 — Gradient descent
text:
Write the gradient descent update rule from memory and say what each symbol in it does.
Minimise a function of one variable in code, and diagnose from the printed path whether the learning rate is too large, too small, or about right.
Explain why the same algorithm started from two different places returns two different answers, and when that matters.

title: 11  Exercise 3.3 — Gradient descent
section: 11.2 Why this, here
text:
11.2 Why this, here
Chapter 10 found the lowest point of a loss surface by evaluating 15,251 candidate lines. That works for two parameters and nothing larger. Every model you will meet after this week — logistic regression on Day 4, and anything with a neural network in it afterwards — is fitted by the method on this page instead: start somewhere, measure which way is downhill, take a step, repeat.

title: 11  Exercise 3.3 — Gradient descent
section: 11.3 The update rule
text:
11.3 The update rule
\[x_{n+1} = x_n - \alpha f'(x_n)\]

\(x_n\) is the current guess.
\(f'(x_n)\) is the derivative of the function at that guess — the slope.
\(\alpha\) is the learning rate: a small positive number controlling step size.

The minus sign carries the whole idea. Where the slope is positive the function rises to the right, so we subtract and move left; where it is negative we subtract a negative and move right. Either way the step is against the slope, and the steeper the slope the bigger the step.

title: 11  Exercise 3.3 — Gradient descent
section: 11.4 Minimising \(f(x) = x^2\)
text:
11.4 Minimising \(f(x) = x^2\)
The derivative is \(f'(x) = 2x\), so the rule becomes \(x_{n+1} = x_n - 2\alpha
x_n\). We know the answer is \(x = 0\), which is why this is the example: you can see whether the algorithm is working.

RPython



library(ggplot2); library(dplyr); library(patchwork)

f       <- function(x) x^2
f_prime <- function(x) 2 * x

curve_df <- data.frame(x = seq(-10, 10, length.out = 200)) |>
  mutate(f_x = f(x), f_prime_x = f_prime(x))

p1 <- ggplot(curve_df, aes(x, f_x)) + geom_line(colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = expression(f(x) == x^2), y = "f(x)")
p2 <- ggplot(curve_df, aes(x, f_prime_x)) + geom_line(colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = expression(paste(f, "'", (x) == 2 * x)), y = "f'(x)")
p1 + p2











import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

f       = lambda x: x**2
f_prime = lambda x: 2 * x

xs = np.linspace(-10, 10, 200)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.5))
axes[0].plot(xs, f(xs), color="steelblue");  axes[0].set_title("f(x) = x^2")
axes[1].plot(xs, f_prime(xs), color="firebrick"); axes[1].set_title("f'(x) = 2x")
for ax in axes:
    ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.8); ax.axvline(0, color="black", lw=0.8)
    ax.set_xlabel("x")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()











Start at \(x = -10\) with \(\alpha = 0.8\) and take ten steps.

RPython



alpha <- 0.8
x     <- -10
path  <- numeric(10)

for (i in 1:10) {
  x       <- x - alpha * f_prime(x)
  path[i] <- x
  cat("step", i, ": x =", signif(x, 4), " f(x) =", signif(f(x), 4), "\n")
}

#> step 1 : x = 6  f(x) = 36 
#> step 2 : x = -3.6  f(x) = 12.96 
#> step 3 : x = 2.16  f(x) = 4.666 
#> step 4 : x = -1.296  f(x) = 1.68 
#> step 5 : x = 0.7776  f(x) = 0.6047 
#> step 6 : x = -0.4666  f(x) = 0.2177 
#> step 7 : x = 0.2799  f(x) = 0.07836 
#> step 8 : x = -0.168  f(x) = 0.02821 
#> step 9 : x = 0.1008  f(x) = 0.01016 
#> step 10 : x = -0.06047  f(x) = 0.003656





alpha = 0.8
x     = -10.0
path  = []

for i in range(1, 11):
    x = x - alpha * f_prime(x)
    path.append(x)
    print(f"step {i}: x = {x:.4g}  f(x) = {f(x):.4g}")

#> step 1: x = 6  f(x) = 36
#> step 2: x = -3.6  f(x) = 12.96
#> step 3: x = 2.16  f(x) = 4.666
#> step 4: x = -1.296  f(x) = 1.68
#> step 5: x = 0.7776  f(x) = 0.6047
#> step 6: x = -0.4666  f(x) = 0.2177
#> step 7: x = 0.2799  f(x) = 0.07836
#> step 8: x = -0.168  f(x) = 0.02821
#> step 9: x = 0.1008  f(x) = 0.01016
#> step 10: x = -0.06047  f(x) = 0.003656





The guess goes −10, 6, −3.6, 2.16, −1.296 and so on: it crosses the minimum every single step and lands closer each time. Overshooting is not failure. With \(\alpha = 0.8\) each step is 1.6 times the distance to the minimum, so the sign flips and the magnitude shrinks by 0.6.

RPython



steps_df <- data.frame(step = 1:10, x = path) |> mutate(f_x = f(x))

ggplot(curve_df, aes(x, f_x)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(data = steps_df, aes(x = x, y = f_x, fill = step),
             shape = 21, size = 3, colour = "black") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "yellow", high = "red") +
  labs(x = "x", y = "f(x)", fill = "step")











fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(xs, f(xs), color="grey")

                cmap="autumn_r", edgecolor="black", zorder=3)
fig.colorbar(sc, ax=ax, label="step")

#> <matplotlib.colorbar.Colorbar object at 0x30536d5d0>

ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("f(x)")
plt.show()

11.5 Task 1 — Your turn, on a function whose minimum you can check
Minimise
\[f(x) = x^2 + 3x + 5\]
Differentiate it on paper first: you should get \(f'(x) = 2x + 3\), which is zero at \(x = -1.5\). Then write the loop and see whether the algorithm agrees with your algebra.

RPython

  x <- x - ______ * g_prime(x)
}

TipStuck?





The derivative of \(ax^2\) is \(2ax\), the derivative of \(bx\) is \(b\), and the derivative of a constant is zero. The second blank is the step size, which is already defined above the loop.






# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.

Forty steps get you to −1.4995. The algorithm approaches the minimum and never arrives, which is true of gradient descent in general: you stop when the improvement stops mattering, not when the gradient is zero.

title: 11  Exercise 3.3 — Gradient descent
section: 11.6 The learning rate is the whole game
text:
11.6 The learning rate is the whole game
Run the same problem — \(f(x) = x^2\) from \(x = -10\) — at four learning rates for twenty steps each.

RPython



descend_1d <- function(alpha, x0 = -10, n = 20) {
  x <- x0
  for (i in seq_len(n)) x <- x - alpha * f_prime(x)
  x
}

rates <- c(0.01, 0.1, 0.8, 1.0, 1.05)
data.frame(alpha = rates,
           final_x = sapply(rates, descend_1d),
           final_f = sapply(rates, function(a) f(descend_1d(a))))

#>   alpha       final_x      final_f
#> 1  0.01 -6.676080e+00 4.457004e+01
#> 2  0.10 -1.152922e-01 1.329228e-02
#> 3  0.80 -3.656158e-04 1.336749e-07
#> 4  1.00 -1.000000e+01 1.000000e+02
#> 5  1.05 -6.727500e+01 4.525926e+03





import pandas as pd

def descend_1d(alpha, x0=-10.0, n=20):
    x = x0
    for _ in range(n):
        x = x - alpha * f_prime(x)
    return x

rates = [0.01, 0.1, 0.8, 1.0, 1.05]
pd.DataFrame({"alpha": rates,
              "final_x": [descend_1d(a) for a in rates],
              "final_f": [f(descend_1d(a)) for a in rates]})

#>    alpha    final_x       final_f
#> 0   0.01  -6.676080  4.457004e+01
#> 1   0.10  -0.115292  1.329228e-02
#> 2   0.80  -0.000366  1.336749e-07
#> 3   1.00 -10.000000  1.000000e+02
#> 4   1.05 -67.274999  4.525926e+03





Read that table carefully, because every row is a different lesson.








\(\alpha\)
After 20 steps
What happened




0.01
\(x = -6.68\)
correct direction, far too slow — it needs thousands of steps


0.1
\(x = -0.115\)
steady approach from one side


0.8
\(x = -0.00037\)
overshoots every step and converges fastest of the five


1.0
\(x = -10\)
bounces between −10 and 10 for ever, making no progress at all


1.05
\(x = -67.3\)
diverges: each step is further out than the last



The fastest rate here is not the smallest one, and the boundary between working and diverging is sharp. For \(f(x)=x^2\) the step multiplies the distance to the minimum by \((1 - 2\alpha)\), so anything below 1 converges, 1 exactly cycles, and above 1 explodes. There is no warning and no error message: at \(\alpha = 1.05\) the loop runs happily and returns a number.






WarningA run that finished is not a run that worked



Nothing in any of those five runs raised an error. If you only look at the final number, the diverging run and the converging run are indistinguishable in form — both are a number. Always print the path, or the loss, and look at whether it is going down.

title: 11  Exercise 3.3 — Gradient descent
section: 11.8 Local and global minima
text:
11.8 Local and global minima
Everything above had one minimum. Now take
\[f(x) = x^4 + x^3 - 2x^2 \qquad f'(x) = 4x^3 + 3x^2 - 4x\]
which has two: a shallow one near \(x = 0.69\) and a deeper one near \(x = -1.44\).

RPython



h       <- function(x) x^4 + x^3 - 2 * x^2
h_prime <- function(x) 4 * x^3 + 3 * x^2 - 4 * x

descend_h <- function(x0, alpha = 0.03, n = 200) {
  x <- x0
  for (i in seq_len(n)) x <- x - alpha * h_prime(x)
  c(start = x0, end = x, f_end = h(x))
}

t(sapply(c(1, 0.2, 0, -0.1, -0.5, 2), descend_h))

#>      start        end      f_end
#> [1,]   1.0  0.6930005 -0.3970463
#> [2,]   0.2  0.6930005 -0.3970463
#> [3,]   0.0  0.0000000  0.0000000
#> [4,]  -0.1 -1.4430005 -2.8334224
#> [5,]  -0.5 -1.4430005 -2.8334224
#> [6,]   2.0  0.6930005 -0.3970463





h       = lambda x: x**4 + x**3 - 2 * x**2
h_prime = lambda x: 4 * x**3 + 3 * x**2 - 4 * x

def descend_h(x0, alpha=0.03, n=200):
    x = float(x0)
    for _ in range(n):
        x = x - alpha * h_prime(x)
    return {"start": x0, "end": x, "f_end": h(x)}

pd.DataFrame([descend_h(s) for s in (1, 0.2, 0, -0.1, -0.5, 2)])

#>    start    end     f_end
#> 0    1.0  0.693 -0.397046
#> 1    0.2  0.693 -0.397046
#> 2    0.0  0.000  0.000000
#> 3   -0.1 -1.443 -2.833422
#> 4   -0.5 -1.443 -2.833422
#> 5    2.0  0.693 -0.397046






RPython



curve_h <- data.frame(x = seq(-2, 1.5, length.out = 300)) |> mutate(f_x = h(x))
ends    <- data.frame(start = c(1, 0.2, 0, -0.1, -0.5, 2)) |>
  mutate(end = sapply(start, function(s) descend_h(s)[["end"]]), f_end = h(end))

ggplot(curve_h, aes(x, f_x)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(data = ends, aes(x = end, y = f_end), colour = "red", size = 3) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "f(x)")











grid_h = np.linspace(-2, 1.5, 300)
ends = [descend_h(s)["end"] for s in (1, 0.2, 0, -0.1, -0.5, 2)]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(grid_h, h(grid_h), color="grey")
ax.scatter(ends, [h(e) for e in ends], color="red", zorder=3)
ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("f(x)")
plt.show()











Starting at 1, 0.2 or 2 lands on \(x = 0.693\), where \(f = -0.397\). Starting at −0.1 or −0.5 lands on \(x = -1.443\), where \(f = -2.833\) — seven times lower. Nothing distinguishes the two runs except where they began, and neither run can tell you it stopped in the worse of the two places.
Starting at exactly 0 is the strangest case: the derivative there is zero, so the first step moves nowhere and every step after it moves nowhere. Gradient descent stops at any stationary point, and \(x = 0\) here is a local maximum.






NoteWhy this does not ruin least squares



The MSE surface you plotted in Chapter 10 is a bowl with one minimum — convex, in the technical term — so for linear regression this whole worry is moot: every starting point reaches the same answer. The worry is real for almost everything else, which is why deep learning papers report random seeds, and why “we trained it twice and got different models” is a sentence you will hear.

title: 11  Exercise 3.3 — Gradient descent
section: 11.10 Two parameters at once
text:
11.10 Two parameters at once
A loss has as many derivatives as it has parameters. Collect them into a gradient vector and the update rule is unchanged — it just applies to every parameter simultaneously. For
\[f(x, y) = x\sin(y) + x^2 \qquad
\nabla f = \left\langle \sin(y) + 2x,\; x\cos(y) \right\rangle\]

RPython



fxy <- function(x, y) x * sin(y) + x^2
grad_x <- function(x, y) sin(y) + 2 * x
grad_y <- function(x, y) x * cos(y)

x <- 1; y <- 2; alpha <- 0.01
trace_xy <- data.frame(iter = 0, x = x, y = y, f = fxy(x, y))

for (i in 1:1000) {
  gx <- grad_x(x, y); gy <- grad_y(x, y)
  x <- x - alpha * gx
  y <- y - alpha * gy
  if (i %% 100 == 0)
    trace_xy <- rbind(trace_xy, data.frame(iter = i, x = x, y = y, f = fxy(x, y)))
}
trace_xy

#>     iter         x         y         f
#> 0      0  1.000000  2.000000  1.909297
#> 1    100 -0.242655  2.084195 -0.152491
#> 2    200 -0.428463  1.933253 -0.217045
#> 3    300 -0.474188  1.801955 -0.236721
#> 4    400 -0.490187  1.713580 -0.244915
#> 5    500 -0.496295  1.657935 -0.248103
#> 6    600 -0.498618  1.623729 -0.249300
#> 7    700 -0.499489  1.602895 -0.249742
#> 8    800 -0.499812  1.590248 -0.249905

It reaches \(x = -0.5\), \(y = 1.578\), \(f = -0.25\), which is the exact minimum of this function: for any \(y\) the best \(x\) is \(-\sin(y)/2\), giving \(f = -\sin^2(y)/4\), smallest when \(\sin y = 1\). Notice how much of the progress happens early — after 100 iterations \(f\) is already −0.153, and the remaining 900 buy −0.097.






NotePartial derivatives by hand, and when not to



We differentiated \(f\) twice by hand, once per variable. For a model with a million parameters nobody does that: the derivatives are generated mechanically — symbolically, as a computer algebra system would, or by automatic differentiation, which is what every deep learning framework is at bottom. Knowing that the gradient is just a list of slopes is enough to read those tools’ output.

title: 11  Exercise 3.3 — Gradient descent
section: 11.11 The result that should bother you
text:
11.11 The result that should bother you
Now put the method on the actual problem: find the intercept and slope that minimise the MSE for glucose against age, by gradient descent instead of by lm(). The gradients of \(\text{MSE}(\beta_0, \beta_1) = \frac{1}{m}\sum (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2\) are
\[\frac{\partial \text{MSE}}{\partial \beta_0} = -\frac{2}{m}\sum r_i
\qquad
\frac{\partial \text{MSE}}{\partial \beta_1} = -\frac{2}{m}\sum x_i r_i\]
with \(r_i = y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i\). Chapter 12 derives them.

RPython



library(readr)
diab <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
glu  <- diab |> filter(glucose > 0) |> slice(1:80) |> select(age, glucose)

descend_mse <- function(x, y, alpha, n) {
  b0 <- 0; b1 <- 0
  mse <- numeric(n)
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    r  <- y - (b0 + b1 * x)
    b0 <- b0 - alpha * (-2 * mean(r))
    b1 <- b1 - alpha * (-2 * mean(x * r))
    mse[i] <- mean((y - (b0 + b1 * x))^2)
  }
  list(b0 = b0, b1 = b1, mse = mse)
}

raw <- descend_mse(glu$age, glu$glucose, alpha = 1e-4, n = 1000)
c(intercept = raw$b0, slope = raw$b1, MSE = tail(raw$mse, 1))

#>   intercept       slope         MSE 
#>    3.234060    3.040203 2512.521591

coef(lm(glucose ~ age, data = glu))

#> (Intercept)         age 
#> 110.2979509   0.2886749





import pandas as pd
diab = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
glu = (diab.loc[diab["glucose"] > 0, ["age", "glucose"]]
           .head(80).reset_index(drop=True))

def descend_mse(x, y, alpha, n):
    x, y = np.asarray(x, float), np.asarray(y, float)
    b0 = b1 = 0.0
    mse = np.empty(n)
    for i in range(n):
        r = y - (b0 + b1 * x)
        b0 = b0 - alpha * (-2 * r.mean())
        b1 = b1 - alpha * (-2 * (x * r).mean())
        mse[i] = np.mean((y - (b0 + b1 * x))**2)
    return {"b0": b0, "b1": b1, "mse": mse}

raw = descend_mse(glu["age"], glu["glucose"], alpha=1e-4, n=1000)
raw["b0"], raw["b1"], raw["mse"][-1]

#> (np.float64(3.2340597363518033), np.float64(3.040202790594225), np.float64(2512.5215912023486))





After a thousand iterations the descent reports an intercept of 3.23 and a slope of 3.04, with an MSE of 2513. The correct answer is 110.298 and 0.2887, with an MSE of 847.5. The descent is not close, and it is worse than predicting the mean glucose for everybody, which scores 863.
Three steps of reasoning.

The run did not fail. The MSE went down at every iteration and the loop finished without complaint. Had we only printed the final parameters and drawn a line through the data, the plot would have looked plausible.
The cause is the shape of the surface from Chapter 10: a long diagonal trough, not a round bowl. Age has a mean of 33 and glucose a mean of 120, so the \(\beta_1\) gradient is hundreds of times larger than the \(\beta_0\) one. Any learning rate small enough to keep \(\beta_1\) stable leaves \(\beta_0\) crawling. Raising \(\alpha\) to \(10^{-3}\) does not fix it either — try it, and watch both parameters overflow to infinity within a few hundred steps.
This is the usual failure of gradient descent on raw clinical data: not a wrong answer that announces itself, but a right-shaped answer that is nowhere near the optimum. The published version of this material reported those unconverged numbers as the optimised parameters.

The fix is to standardise both columns — subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation — so the trough becomes a bowl, descend there, and convert the answer back.

title: 11  Exercise 3.3 — Gradient descent
section: 11.12 Task 4 — Make it converge
text:
11.12 Task 4 — Make it converge
Standardise, descend with a learning rate a thousand times larger, and rescale the parameters to the original units.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")

zx <- (glu$age - mean(glu$age)) / sd(glu$age)
zy <- (glu$glucose - ______) / sd(glu$glucose)

std <- descend_mse(zx, zy, alpha = 0.1, n = 50)

slope     <- std$b1 * sd(glu$glucose) / sd(glu$age)
intercept <- mean(glu$glucose) + sd(glu$glucose) * std$b0 - slope * mean(glu$age)

c(intercept = intercept, slope = slope)
check_matches(slope, coef(lm(glucose ~ age, data = glu))[["age"]],
              label = "slope from gradient descent")







TipStuck?





Standardising a column means centring it on its own mean and dividing by its own standard deviation. The line above does it for age; do the same thing to glucose.






# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

mx, sx = glu["age"].mean(), glu["age"].std()
my, sy = glu["glucose"].mean(), glu["glucose"].std()
zx = (glu["age"] - mx) / sx
zy = (glu["glucose"] - ______) / sy

std = descend_mse(zx, zy, alpha=0.1, n=50)

slope     = std["b1"] * sy / sx
intercept = my + sy * std["b0"] - slope * mx

ref = LinearRegression().fit(glu[["age"]], glu["glucose"])
print(intercept, slope)
check_matches(slope, ref.coef_[0], label="slope from gradient descent")




Fifty iterations on the standardised data give 110.298 and 0.28867, agreeing with lm() to five significant figures. The same algorithm, the same data, the same loss; twenty times fewer iterations and a thousand times larger step. Scaling was not a tidying-up step, it was the difference between an answer and no answer.






NoteOne more thing the standardised fit tells you



On standardised columns the fitted slope is 0.1347, which is exactly the correlation between age and glucose. That is not a coincidence, and Chapter 12 shows why.



RPython



std_shown <- descend_mse((glu$age - mean(glu$age)) / sd(glu$age),
                         (glu$glucose - mean(glu$glucose)) / sd(glu$glucose),
                         alpha = 0.1, n = 50)

data.frame(iteration = 1:50, MSE = std_shown$mse) |>
  ggplot(aes(iteration, MSE)) +
  geom_line(colour = "firebrick") +
  labs(x = "Iteration", y = "MSE (standardised units)")











std_shown = descend_mse((glu["age"] - glu["age"].mean()) / glu["age"].std(),
                        (glu["glucose"] - glu["glucose"].mean()) / glu["glucose"].std(),
                        alpha=0.1, n=50)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(range(1, 51), std_shown["mse"], color="firebrick")
ax.set_xlabel("Iteration"); ax.set_ylabel("MSE (standardised units)")
plt.show()











That curve is the plot to draw every time you run an optimiser. A descent that is working looks like this: a steep fall, then a flat tail. Anything else — a rise, a wobble, a straight line still sloping down at the last iteration — is telling you to change the learning rate or the number of steps.

You are handed a fitted model and a plot of its loss against iteration. The curve is still falling at the final iteration. What do you do, and what would you have to check before trusting the model as it stands?

section: 11.15 What you can and cannot now claim
text:
11.15 What you can and cannot now claim
Can: that you can minimise a function numerically in either language, diagnose a learning rate from the loss curve, and state why a converged descent on a convex loss gives the same answer as lm().
Cannot: that you needed any of this for linear regression. For this particular model there is an exact formula, obtainable with algebra and no iteration at all, and that is Chapter 12.

text: 12.1 Objectives

text:

title: 12  Exercise 3.4 — Ordinary least squares, in closed form
section: 12.2 Why this, here
text:
12.2 Why this, here
Chapter 11 minimised the squared-error loss by walking downhill, and needed standardised columns and a well-chosen learning rate to get there. For this particular loss and this particular model, none of that is necessary: the minimum can be written down. This exercise does the algebra, and then checks it against the software.






NoteThis exercise is one language, deliberately



The derivation is algebra and has no R version or Python version. Only the verification at the end is code, and that appears in both languages. If you are following the booklet in Python, the three pages of mathematics below still apply to you in full — LinearRegression is solving the same equations as lm().
crumbs: 12  Exercise 3.4 — Ordinary least squares, in closed form

title: 12  Exercise 3.4 — Ordinary least squares, in closed form
section: 12.3 Setting up the minimisation problem
text:
12.3 Setting up the minimisation problem
We want the intercept and slope that minimise the sum of squared residuals:
\[\min_{\hat{\beta_0}, \hat{\beta_1}} \; W, \qquad\text{where}\qquad
W = \sum_{i=1}^{N} (y_i - \hat{\beta_0} - \hat{\beta_1} x_i)^2 \tag{12.1}\]
Minimising the sum and minimising the mean are the same problem: dividing by \(N\) scales the whole surface without moving its lowest point. We use the sum here because it keeps the algebra clean.
A minimum of a smooth function is where all its partial derivatives vanish. There are two parameters, so there are two equations.
\[\frac{\partial W}{\partial \hat{\beta_0}} =
\sum_{i=1}^{N} -2(y_i - \hat{\beta_0} - \hat{\beta_1} x_i) = 0 \tag{12.2}\]
\[\frac{\partial W}{\partial \hat{\beta_1}} =
\sum_{i=1}^{N} -2 x_i (y_i - \hat{\beta_0} - \hat{\beta_1} x_i) = 0 \tag{12.3}\]
Both follow from the chain rule: the inside of the bracket differentiates to \(-1\) with respect to \(\hat\beta_0\) and to \(-x_i\) with respect to \(\hat\beta_1\). These two are the normal equations, and everything below is rearrangement.






NoteWhere the gradients of Chapter 11 came from



Equation 12.2 and Equation 12.3, divided by \(N\), are exactly the two gradients the descent loop used. The difference between the two exercises is not the mathematics; it is that here we set the derivatives to zero and solve, while there we evaluated them at the current guess and took a step.
crumbs: 12  Exercise 3.4 — Ordinary least squares, in closed form

title: 12  Exercise 3.4 — Ordinary least squares, in closed form
section: 12.4 Solving for \(\hat{\beta_0}\)
text:
12.4 Solving for \(\hat{\beta_0}\)
Divide Equation 12.2 by \(-2\) — which is allowed because the right-hand side is zero, and is the reason some textbooks write the loss with a \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) in front:
\[\sum_{i=1}^{N} (y_i - \hat{\beta_0} - \hat{\beta_1} x_i) = 0\]
Distribute the summation over the three terms. The middle one is a constant summed \(N\) times:
\[\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i - N\hat{\beta_0} - \hat{\beta_1}\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i = 0
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
N \hat{\beta_0} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i - \hat{\beta_1} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i\]
Divide by \(N\) and use \(\frac{1}{N}\sum y_i = \bar{y}\) and \(\frac{1}{N}\sum x_i = \bar{x}\):
\[\boxed{\;\hat{\beta_0} = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta_1} \bar{x}\;}\]
Read that before going on: whatever the slope turns out to be, the fitted line passes through the point \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\). The mean of the predictors and the mean of the outcome are always on the line.
crumbs: 12  Exercise 3.4 — Ordinary least squares, in closed form

title: 12  Exercise 3.4 — Ordinary least squares, in closed form
section: 12.5 Solving for \(\hat{\beta_1}\)
text:
12.5 Solving for \(\hat{\beta_1}\)
Divide Equation 12.3 by \(-2\) as well, and expand:
\[\sum_{i=1}^{N} \left( x_i y_i - \hat{\beta_0} x_i - \hat{\beta_1} x_i^2 \right) = 0\]
Substitute \(\hat{\beta_0} = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta_1} \bar{x}\) from above:
\[\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i y_i - \sum_{i=1}^{N}(\bar{y} - \hat{\beta_1}\bar{x})x_i
- \hat{\beta_1} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i^2 = 0\]
Distribute the sums, pulling the constants \(\bar{x}\) and \(\bar{y}\) out in front:
\[\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i y_i - \bar{y}\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_i
+ \hat{\beta_1}\bar{x} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i - \hat{\beta_1} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i^2 = 0\]
Now collect the two terms in \(\hat{\beta_1}\) on one side and use \(\sum x_i = N\bar{x}\) and \(\sum y_i = N\bar{y}\):
\[\hat{\beta_1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i^2 - N\bar{x}^2\right)
= \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i y_i - N\bar{x}\bar{y}\]
which, using the identity in the callout below for both sides, is
\[\hat{\beta_1} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}
{\sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})^2}
= \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(x,y)}{\operatorname{Var}(x)}\]






NoteThe identity, in six steps





\[\sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i y_i - N \bar{x} \bar{y}\]
Step 1 — expand the product. \[\sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})
= \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left( x_i y_i - x_i \bar{y} - \bar{x} y_i + \bar{x} \bar{y} \right)\]
Step 2 — separate the summation. \[= \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i y_i - \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i \bar{y}
  - \sum_{i=1}^{N} \bar{x} y_i + \sum_{i=1}^{N} \bar{x} \bar{y}\]
Step 3 — factor the constants out. \(\bar{x}\) and \(\bar{y}\) do not depend on \(i\), so \[\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i \bar{y} = \bar{y} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i, \qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{N} \bar{x} y_i = \bar{x} \sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i, \qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{N} \bar{x} \bar{y} = N \bar{x} \bar{y}\]
Step 4 — substitute back. \[= \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i y_i - \bar{y} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i
  - \bar{x} \sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i + N \bar{x} \bar{y}\]
Step 5 — use \(\sum x_i = N \bar{x}\) and \(\sum y_i = N \bar{y}\). \[= \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i y_i - \bar{y} (N \bar{x}) - \bar{x} (N \bar{y})
  + N \bar{x} \bar{y}\]
Step 6 — combine. The second and third terms are each \(-N\bar{x}\bar{y}\), and one of them cancels the fourth: \[= \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i y_i - N \bar{x} \bar{y}\]
Setting \(y = x\) gives the companion identity \(\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 = \sum x_i^2 - N\bar{x}^2\), which is the denominator.



So the complete solution, for one predictor, is two lines of arithmetic:
\[\hat{\beta_1} = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(x,y)}{\operatorname{Var}(x)}
\qquad\qquad
\hat{\beta_0} = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta_1} \bar{x}\]
No iteration, no learning rate, no starting guess. The derivation follows the one in Berkeley’s EEP118 handout; with more than one predictor the same argument is done in matrix form and gives \(\hat{\beta} = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y\), which is what lm() actually evaluates.

12.6 Task 1 — The closed form against the software
Compute both estimators from means, a covariance and a variance, and compare them with the fitted model.

RPython

b1hat <- ______ / ______

TipStuck?





Two functions, cov() and var(), in the order the formula gives them. The third blank is the mean of the predictor.






# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import pandas as pd, numpy as np, sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

diab = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
glu = (diab.loc[diab["glucose"] > 0, ["age", "glucose"]]
           .head(80).reset_index(drop=True))
x, y = glu["age"], glu["glucose"]

b1hat = ______ / ______          # pandas: x.cov(y) and x.var(), both ddof=1
b0hat = y.mean() - b1hat * ______

fit = LinearRegression().fit(glu[["age"]], y)
print({"closed_form": (b0hat, b1hat), "sklearn": (fit.intercept_, fit.coef_[0])})

check_matches(b1hat, fit.coef_[0], tol=1e-8, label="closed-form slope")




Both give 110.298 and 0.2886749. Not approximately: to every digit either language will print. lm() is not doing anything you have not just done by hand, and neither is LinearRegression.






NoteThe covariance ratio also explains Chapter 11



Standardising both columns makes \(\operatorname{Var}(x) = 1\) and turns \(\operatorname{Cov}(x,y)\) into the correlation, so on standardised data \(\hat\beta_1 = \operatorname{Cor}(x,y)\) — the 0.1347 the descent converged to. The correlation is the slope of the standardised fit, which is a more useful definition of it than the one most people carry.

12.7 Task 2 — The two conditions the derivation imposes
Equation 12.2 and Equation 12.3 say that at the optimum, \(\sum r_i = 0\) and \(\sum x_i r_i = 0\). Those are not assumptions about the world; they are consequences of having minimised. Check both for the fitted line, and for the hand-drawn line from Chapter 10.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
r_fitted <- ______                     # residuals of the fitted line
r_guess  <- y - (120 + 0.5 * x)        # residuals of the hand-drawn line

rbind(fitted = c(sum_r = sum(r_fitted), sum_xr = sum(x * r_fitted)),
      guess  = c(sum_r = sum(r_guess),  sum_xr = sum(x * r_guess)))

check_matches(sum(r_fitted), 0, tol = 1e-6, label = "sum of fitted residuals")




# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
r_fitted = ______                      # residuals of the fitted line
r_guess  = y - (120 + 0.5 * x)

print({"fitted": (r_fitted.sum(), (x * r_fitted).sum()),
       "guess":  (r_guess.sum(),  (x * r_guess).sum())})

check_matches(r_fitted.sum(), 0, tol=1e-6, label="sum of fitted residuals")




The fitted residuals sum to something of the order of \(10^{-13}\) and their product with age to the order of \(10^{-11}\): zero, to the precision floating-point arithmetic allows. The hand-drawn line’s residuals sum to −1338.5 and its cross-product to −47700.5.
That is a diagnostic worth keeping. If someone hands you fitted values from a least-squares model and the residuals do not sum to zero, either there is no intercept in the model or those are not least-squares fitted values.
