title: 12  Exercise 3.4 — Ordinary least squares, in closed form
section: 12.8 The result that should bother you
text:
12.8 The result that should bother you
The derivation divides by \(\operatorname{Var}(x)\). It therefore returns an answer for any dataset in which the predictor is not perfectly constant — and says nothing about how large that variance is. Refit the same model on progressively narrower age bands.

RPython



bands <- list(c(21, 25), c(21, 30), c(21, 40), c(21, 81))

do.call(rbind, lapply(bands, function(b) {
  s <- glu |> filter(age >= b[1], age <= b[2])
  data.frame(band = paste(b[1], "to", b[2]), n = nrow(s),
             var_age = var(s$age),
             slope = cov(s$age, s$glucose) / var(s$age))
}))

#>       band  n    var_age     slope
#> 1 21 to 25 32   1.910282 0.6812665
#> 2 21 to 30 48   8.074025 4.1727148
#> 3 21 to 40 59  21.303916 2.2139585
#> 4 21 to 81 80 190.398576 0.2886749





rows = []
for lo, hi in [(21, 25), (21, 30), (21, 40), (21, 81)]:
    s = glu[(glu["age"] >= lo) & (glu["age"] <= hi)]
    rows.append({"band": f"{lo} to {hi}", "n": len(s),
                 "var_age": s["age"].var(),
                 "slope": s["age"].cov(s["glucose"]) / s["age"].var()})
pd.DataFrame(rows)

#>        band   n     var_age     slope
#> 0  21 to 25  32    1.910282  0.681266
#> 1  21 to 30  48    8.074025  4.172715
#> 2  21 to 40  59   21.303916  2.213958
#> 3  21 to 81  80  190.398576  0.288675





Three steps of reasoning.

Over the full range the slope is 0.289 mg/dL per year. Among patients aged 21 to 40 it is 2.21, and among those aged 21 to 30 it is 4.17 — fourteen times the full-range estimate, from a subset of the same 80 patients.
The mechanism is the denominator. Restricting the age range cuts \(\operatorname{Var}(x)\) from 190 to 8, and the covariance in the numerator is estimated from fewer, closer points, so it is noise-dominated. The estimator is behaving exactly as derived; the data cannot support what is being asked of it.
So a published slope is not a property of a relationship. It is a property of a relationship and the range of predictor values the sample happened to cover. When you compare your coefficient with someone else’s, compare the predictor ranges first.

12.10 Reflection

The derivation never mentions the data being normally distributed, independent, or anything else. What exactly does it assume, and where in the algebra would you look to find out?
Given that the closed form exists and takes microseconds, why is the whole of modern machine learning fitted by gradient descent?

title: 13  Exercise 4.1 — One interface, many models
section: 13.2 Why this, here
text:
13.2 Why this, here
In Chapter 2 you wrote the five steps out by hand, with lm() in R and LinearRegression() in Python. That is affordable for one model. From today the models multiply — logistic regression now, trees and forests on Day 5 — and each one of them has its own function name, its own argument names and its own way of returning a prediction. rpart() wants method = "class"; randomForest() wants the outcome to be a factor and will quietly do regression if it is not; glmnet() refuses a formula and demands a matrix.
Two ecosystems exist to put one interface in front of all of that: tidymodels in R and scikit-learn in Python. The point of this exercise is not that they save typing. It is that they make models comparable: when the only line that differs between two analyses is the one naming the model, the difference in the result is attributable to the model.








The question
tidymodels
scikit-learn




what kind of model is this
logistic_reg(), decision_tree()
the estimator class, LogisticRegression


which code actually fits it
set_engine("glm")
the class, plus solver=


what happens to the data first
a recipe() of step_*()
transformers, e.g. StandardScaler


the two bolted together
workflow()
Pipeline


fit it, then use it
fit(), predict()
.fit(), .predict()

title: 13  Exercise 4.1 — One interface, many models
section: 13.3 A specification is not a model
text:
13.3 A specification is not a model
Declaring a model and fitting it are separate acts, and both frameworks make you notice. In R you can print a specification that has never seen data. In Python the estimator exists, but asking it to predict raises an error until you fit it.

RPython



library(tidymodels)

log_spec  <- logistic_reg(mode = "classification") |> set_engine("glm")
tree_spec <- decision_tree(mode = "classification") |> set_engine("rpart")

log_spec

#> Logistic Regression Model Specification (classification)
#> 
#> Computational engine: glm





from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.exceptions import NotFittedError

log_spec = LogisticRegression(C=float("inf"), max_iter=1000)

try:
    log_spec.predict([[120.0, 30.0, 40.0]])
except NotFittedError as e:
    print(str(e).split(".")[0])

#> This LogisticRegression instance is not fitted yet





The R specification says logistic regression, fitted by glm and nothing else: no data, no coefficients. Swapping "glm" for "glmnet" keeps the first half and replaces the second.

title: 13  Exercise 4.1 — One interface, many models
section: 13.4 The split we use all day
text:
13.4 The split we use all day
data/diabetes.csv holds 768 adults screened for type 2 diabetes: eight measurements from a single visit and diabetes, which is pos or neg.
We hold back every fifth row. That is not how you would usually split, and the reason we do it here is worth a paragraph.






NoteWhy a fixed rule rather than a seed



Chapter 2 showed that set.seed(42) and random_state=42 select different rows, so the two languages ended the day with different test sets and different scores. That is honest, but it means any R-versus-Python difference you then see is confounded with the split.
Taking every fifth row of a file whose row order carries no information gives both languages the same 153 patients, so the rest of this day compares languages rather than partitions. Exercise 1.2’s Stretch 2 asked how much the split matters; Stretch 1 below is that question again, and the answer is still “more than you would like”.



RPython



library(readr); library(dplyr)

diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

test_rows <- seq(5, nrow(diabetes), by = 5)
train <- diabetes[-test_rows, ]
test  <- diabetes[ test_rows, ]

c(train = nrow(train), test = nrow(test), test_pos = sum(test$diabetes == "pos"))

#>    train     test test_pos 
#>      615      153       55





import pandas as pd

diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")

is_test = (diabetes.index + 1) % 5 == 0
train, test = diabetes[~is_test], diabetes[is_test]

y_train = (train["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)
y_test  = (test["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)
features = ["glucose", "mass", "age"]

len(train), len(test), int(y_test.sum())

#> (615, 153, 55)

title: 13  Exercise 4.1 — One interface, many models
section: 13.5 Fit and predict: the same two verbs, whatever the model
text:
13.5 Fit and predict: the same two verbs, whatever the model

RPython



log_fit  <- log_spec  |> fit(diabetes ~ glucose + mass + age, data = train)
tree_fit <- tree_spec |> fit(diabetes ~ glucose + mass + age, data = train)

acc <- function(f) mean(predict(f, test)$.pred_class == test$diabetes)
c(logistic = acc(log_fit), tree = acc(tree_fit),
  majority = mean(test$diabetes == "neg"))

#>  logistic      tree  majority 
#> 0.7124183 0.6928105 0.6405229





from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

log_fit  = LogisticRegression(C=float("inf"), max_iter=1000).fit(train[features], y_train)
tree_fit = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42).fit(train[features], y_train)

{"logistic": round(log_fit.score(test[features], y_test), 4),
 "tree":     round(tree_fit.score(test[features], y_test), 4),
 "majority": round(float((y_test == 0).mean()), 4)}

#> {'logistic': 0.7124, 'tree': 0.5948, 'majority': 0.6405}





Two readings, and the second is the uncomfortable one.
The logistic regressions agree: 0.712 in both languages, on the same 153 patients. The trees do not — about 0.69 in R against about 0.59 in Python — and the word decision_tree is identical in both. rpart stops growing when a split stops paying for itself, so it returns ten leaves; DecisionTreeClassifier grows until every leaf is pure, so it returns about 180 and scores 1.00 on the rows it was fitted to. Same name, same data, different default, and the default is the whole difference. Chapter 19 is where you learn to control it.
And a third reading, which should take the shine off all of them: always saying neg scores 0.641 on this test set. The logistic model’s seven percentage points over that is the entire return on three clinical measurements.

13.6 Task 1 — Swap the model, keep everything else
Fit a third model — a random forest, five hundred trees instead of one — on the same rows, and score it against the majority baseline. One line names the model; nothing else changes.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
rf_fit <- rand_forest(mode = "classification") |>
  set_engine("ranger", seed = 42) |>
  fit(______, data = ______)

acc_rf <- mean(predict(rf_fit, test)$.pred_class == test$diabetes)
check_beats_prevalence(acc_rf, test$diabetes)




# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

rf_fit = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42).fit(______, ______)

acc_rf = rf_fit.score(test[features], y_test)
check_beats_prevalence(acc_rf, y_test)










TipStuck?





The R side wants the same formula and the same data frame you gave fit() for the logistic model. The Python side wants the predictor columns and the outcome as two separate arguments — that is the shape difference from Exercise 1.1, and it has not gone away.



A forest has no coefficients, no equation and no way of telling a clinician why it said what it said. It also, here, does not win: five hundred trees score about 0.69–0.70 against the logistic regression’s 0.712 on the same rows. Note that down before Chapter 20, and note too that the cost of finding it out was one line — which is the argument for the framework, and the only argument this exercise is making.

title: 13  Exercise 4.1 — One interface, many models
section: 13.7 Task 2 — Swap the engine, keep the model
text:
13.7 Task 2 — Swap the engine, keep the model
Now change only the second half of the specification. In R, replace the glm engine with glmnet, which fits the same logistic model with a penalty on the coefficients. In Python there is no engine slot; the nearest thing is solver=, so change that instead and see whether it does the same job.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
lasso_fit <- logistic_reg(penalty = 0.1, mixture = 1) |>
  set_engine("______") |>
  fit(diabetes ~ glucose + mass + age, data = train)

round(coef(lasso_fit$fit, s = 0.1)[, 1], 5)   # compare with the glm coefficients
round(coef(log_fit$fit), 5)




# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import numpy as np
for solver in ["lbfgs", "newton-cg", "______"]:
    m = LogisticRegression(C=1.0, solver=solver, max_iter=1000).fit(train[features], y_train)
    print(f"{solver:>10}", np.round(m.coef_[0], 5), round(m.intercept_[0], 3))




In R the engine change is a change of model: the lasso drives the coefficients for mass and age to exactly zero and keeps only glucose. Two of your three predictors have left the building, and nothing in the specification said they could.
In Python two of the three solvers agree to four decimal places and the third, liblinear, does not — it penalises the intercept as well, which the other two do not. So “the solver is only a numerical detail” is true twice out of three times, which is the worst possible number of times for a thing to be true.

title: 13  Exercise 4.1 — One interface, many models
section: 13.8 Task 3 — Put preprocessing inside the model object
text:
13.8 Task 3 — Put preprocessing inside the model object
A workflow and a Pipeline are the same idea: one object that remembers both what you did to the data and what you fitted to it, so that the identical treatment reaches the test rows. Build one with the predictors standardised.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
rec <- recipe(diabetes ~ glucose + mass + age, data = train) |>
  step_normalize(______)

wf_fit <- workflow() |>
  add_model(log_spec) |>
  add_recipe(______) |>
  fit(data = train)

acc_wf <- mean(predict(wf_fit, test)$.pred_class == test$diabetes)
check_beats_prevalence(acc_wf, test$diabetes)
round(coef(extract_fit_engine(wf_fit)), 4)




# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

pipe = Pipeline([
    ("scale", ______),
    ("model", LogisticRegression(C=float("inf"), max_iter=1000)),
]).fit(train[features], y_train)

acc_pipe = pipe.score(test[features], y_test)
check_beats_prevalence(acc_pipe, y_test)
np.round(pipe[-1].coef_[0], 4), round(pipe[-1].intercept_[0], 4)










NoteAssign the result of .fit(), always



Written as a bare line, pipe.fit(X, y) returns the fitted pipeline, and both Jupyter and this booklet will then print scikit-learn’s HTML representation of it — the grey box listing every default parameter. It is noise in a notebook, and in a knitr render under a non-UTF-8 locale it stops the build outright. Assign the result, or end the line with a semicolon.


Compare the standardised coefficients with the unstandardised ones from the earlier cell. The accuracy is unchanged at 0.712 — an unpenalised logistic regression does not care about the units of its predictors — but the coefficients now say something the originals could not: per standard deviation, glucose carries about four times the weight of mass or age.






NoteTwo things differ between the languages here, and only one matters



R reports the standardised glucose coefficient as about 1.1804 and Python as about 1.1794. The cause is that step_normalize() divides by the sample standard deviation (dividing by \(n-1\)) and StandardScaler by the population one (dividing by \(n\)). It is a convention, it is a fourth decimal place, and it never changed a clinical conclusion.
The difference that does matter is in the next section.
The reason to put the scaling inside the object rather than before the split is leakage: a scaler fitted on all 768 rows has read the test set’s mean. That is Chapter 7’s subject and this is the machinery that prevents it.

title: 13  Exercise 4.1 — One interface, many models
section: 13.9 The result that should bother you
text:
13.9 The result that should bother you
The two frameworks give you the same interface. They do not give you the same model.

On these 615 training rows, R’s glm and scikit-learn with C=inf agree to five decimal places: glucose 0.03508, mass 0.03598, age 0.02170. Whatever else is going on, the two libraries solve the same problem when you ask them to.
But C=inf is not scikit-learn’s default. The default is C=1.0, which is an L2 penalty on the coefficients — the thing the glmnet engine does in R only when you ask for it. On 615 rows the penalty is swamped by the likelihood and you cannot see it.
Run the cell below, which refits on the first 50 rows only. Now you can.


RPython



small <- diabetes[1:50, ]
z <- function(x) (x - mean(x)) / sd(x)
glm_small <- glm(diabetes ~ z(glucose) + z(mass) + z(age) + z(pedigree),
                 data = small, family = binomial)
round(coef(glm_small), 3)

#> (Intercept)  z(glucose)     z(mass)      z(age) z(pedigree) 
#>      -1.118       0.799      -0.022       0.101       0.968





from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import numpy as np

small = diabetes.iloc[:50]
y_small = (small["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)
f4 = ["glucose", "mass", "age", "pedigree"]

for C, label in [(float("inf"), "no penalty"), (1.0, "the default")]:
    p = Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()),
                  ("model", LogisticRegression(C=C, max_iter=2000))]).fit(small[f4], y_small)
    print(f"{label:>12}", dict(zip(f4, np.round(p[-1].coef_[0], 3))))

#>   no penalty {'glucose': np.float64(0.791), 'mass': np.float64(-0.022), 'age': np.float64(0.1), 'pedigree': np.float64(0.959)}
#>  the default {'glucose': np.float64(0.663), 'mass': np.float64(0.035), 'age': np.float64(0.117), 'pedigree': np.float64(0.751)}





Unpenalised, mass has a coefficient of −0.022; at the default C=1.0 it is +0.035. Fifty patients, four predictors, and the sign of a clinical association depends on an argument nobody typed. R’s unpenalised glm gives −0.022 too: it matches the unpenalised Python fit, not Python’s default.
The lesson is not that scikit-learn is wrong — a penalty on 50 rows is good statistics, and Day 5 will argue for it. The lesson is that “I fitted a logistic regression” does not identify a model, and a methods section that says only that cannot be reproduced in the other language.

section: 13.12 What you can and cannot now claim
text:
13.12 What you can and cannot now claim
Can: that you can fit, swap and score models through one interface in either language, and that you know which line to change to swap the algorithm, the engine or the preprocessing.
Cannot: that any of these models is any good. Every number on this page is an accuracy, and accuracy on a 36% prevalence outcome is a weak instrument — 0.641 of it is free. Before judging a classifier you need to know what it predicts for an individual patient, which is a probability, and that is Chapter 14.

crumbs: 14  Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve

title: 14  Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve
section: 14.2 Why this, here
text:
14.2 Why this, here
Chapter 13 fitted four classifiers and scored them all with accuracy, which is a property of a whole test set. No clinician has ever treated a test set. The object a clinician meets is a single patient with a single number attached, and for logistic regression that number is a probability — which is why this is the model the booklet uses to learn classification, long before the more accurate ones.
Getting from a linear model to a probability needs one idea, and the idea is arithmetic rather than statistics.
crumbs: 14  Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve

title: 14  Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve
section: 14.3 Probability, odds, log-odds
text:
14.3 Probability, odds, log-odds

RPython



p <- 0.8
odds <- p / (1 - p)
logit <- log(odds)
c(probability = p, odds = odds, log_odds = logit)

#> probability        odds    log_odds 
#>    0.800000    4.000000    1.386294





import numpy as np

p = 0.8
odds = p / (1 - p)
logit = np.log(odds)
{"probability": p, "odds": odds, "log_odds": round(float(logit), 4)}

#> {'probability': 0.8, 'odds': 4.000000000000001, 'log_odds': 1.3863}





Three names for the same belief, on three different scales.

A probability lives in \([0, 1]\).
The odds, \(p/(1-p)\), live in \([0, \infty)\). A probability of 0.8 is odds of 4, usually said as “four to one on”.
The log-odds or logit, \(\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)\), live on the whole real line.

Only the third is a scale a linear model can safely be written on: a linear predictor is unbounded, and so are the log-odds. That single sentence is the whole reason logistic regression has the form it does.
\[\operatorname{logit}(p) = \log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\]
and running it backwards gives the logistic (sigmoid) function
\[p = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x)}}.\]






NoteThis bit has no language



The two equations above are algebra, so there is no R version and no Python version of them. Everything below is both. Deriving the second from the first takes three lines and is the only derivation in today’s material; do it once, on paper, and you will never again be unsure which way round exp goes.
crumbs: 14  Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve

title: 14  Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve
section: 14.4 Fit it, in both languages, to the same rows
text:
14.4 Fit it, in both languages, to the same rows
data/diabetes.csv again, all 768 patients, one predictor. We are not splitting here, and the reason is not laziness: this exercise reads the shape of a fitted curve and the meaning of a coefficient, neither of which is a claim about unseen patients. The moment we make such a claim — the next exercise — the split comes back.

RPython



library(readr); library(dplyr); library(tidymodels)

diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

fit_glucose <- logistic_reg() |>
  set_engine("glm") |>
  fit(diabetes ~ glucose, data = diabetes)

tidy(fit_glucose)

#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>   term        estimate std.error statistic  p.value
#>   <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 (Intercept)  -5.10     0.400       -12.8 3.09e-37
#> 2 glucose       0.0355   0.00302      11.8 5.89e-32





import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
y = (diabetes["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)
X = diabetes[["glucose"]]

fit_glucose = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf, max_iter=1000).fit(X, y)
float(fit_glucose.intercept_[0]), float(fit_glucose.coef_[0][0])

#> (-5.0953569044194404, 0.03548515592234879)





Both give an intercept of −5.09536 and a glucose coefficient of 0.035485. They agree to every digit printed because they are now solving the same problem: C=np.inf switches off the L2 penalty that scikit-learn applies by default, and which R’s glm never applies at all (Chapter 13).






WarningC=np.inf, and what to do if your scikit-learn complains



Older versions of scikit-learn spell the same thing penalty=None, and versions from 1.8 deprecate that spelling in favour of C=np.inf. If you leave the argument out altogether you will get a slightly different, penalised fit and the two languages will stop agreeing — on this dataset in the fourth decimal place, on a small one in the first.


The fitted model is therefore
\[\operatorname{logit}\big(P(\text{diabetes} = \text{pos} \mid \text{glucose})\big)
= -5.095 + 0.0355 \times \text{glucose}.\]

title: 14  Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve
section: 14.5 Task 1 — Say the coefficient out loud
text:
14.5 Task 1 — Say the coefficient out loud
A log-odds coefficient is not interpretable as it stands, and 0.0355 per mg/dL is not a sentence anyone would say. Exponentiating turns it into an odds ratio, and a 10 mg/dL step is a clinically sensible unit. Produce the odds ratio for a 10 mg/dL rise in glucose.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
beta_glucose <- coef(fit_glucose$fit)[["glucose"]]
or_10 <- ______(10 * beta_glucose)
check_metric_range(or_10, 1.2, 1.7, "odds ratio per 10 mg/dL")




# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
beta_glucose = fit_glucose.coef_[0][0]
or_10 = ______(10 * beta_glucose)
check_metric_range(or_10, 1.2, 1.7, "odds ratio per 10 mg/dL")










TipStuck?





The coefficient is on the log-odds scale and you want the odds scale. One function undoes a logarithm.



Write the sentence the number supports, in full: every 10 mg/dL of glucose multiplies the odds of diabetes by about 1.43. Then write what it does not support. It is not a risk ratio, it is not an effect of glucose on anything, and it is not a 43% increase in the probability — which the next task makes uncomfortably concrete.

title: 14  Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve
section: 14.6 Task 2 — One patient, by hand and by machine
text:
14.6 Task 2 — One patient, by hand and by machine
A patient presents with a glucose of 120. Compute their log-odds, odds and probability from the two coefficients, using nothing but arithmetic. Then ask the fitted object for the same probability and check the two agree.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
b <- coef(fit_glucose$fit)

log_odds_120 <- b[["(Intercept)"]] + b[["glucose"]] * ______
odds_120     <- exp(log_odds_120)
prob_120     <- 1 / (1 + exp(______))

by_machine <- predict(fit_glucose,
                      new_data = tibble(glucose = 120),
                      type = "prob")$.pred_pos

round(c(log_odds = log_odds_120, odds = odds_120,
        prob = prob_120, by_machine = by_machine), 4)
check_metric_range(prob_120, 0.25, 0.35, "P(pos | glucose = 120)")




# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
b0, b1 = fit_glucose.intercept_[0], fit_glucose.coef_[0][0]

log_odds_120 = b0 + b1 * ______
odds_120     = np.exp(log_odds_120)
prob_120     = 1 / (1 + np.exp(______))

by_machine = fit_glucose.predict_proba(pd.DataFrame({"glucose": [120]}))[0, 1]

print(np.round([log_odds_120, odds_120, prob_120, by_machine], 4))
check_metric_range(prob_120, 0.25, 0.35, "P(pos | glucose = 120)")




The answer is a probability of about 0.302: log-odds −0.837, odds 0.433. Now compare it with the sentence from Task 1. The odds ratio of 1.43 per 10 mg/dL is constant for every patient; the change in probability for the same 10 mg/dL is not. Going from 120 to 130 moves the probability by about 8 percentage points; going from 60 to 70 moves it by about 2. The model is linear in the log-odds and in nothing else, which is exactly what the sigmoid’s shape is telling you.

title: 14  Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve
section: 14.7 Task 3 — Draw the curve over the data
text:
14.7 Task 3 — Draw the curve over the data
Plot the predicted probability against glucose, with the observed outcomes drawn at 0 and 1 underneath. This is the plot to have in your head whenever anyone says “the model predicts diabetes”.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
library(ggplot2)
preds <- predict(fit_glucose, new_data = diabetes, type = "prob") |>
  bind_cols(diabetes) |>
  mutate(observed = if_else(diabetes == "pos", ______, 0))

ggplot(preds, aes(x = glucose)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = observed), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ______), colour = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Glucose (mg/dL)", y = "Observed class (0/1) and P(pos)")




# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
diabetes["p_pos"] = fit_glucose.predict_proba(X)[:, ______]
ordered = diabetes.sort_values("glucose")

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(diabetes["glucose"], y, alpha=0.2)
ax.plot(ordered["glucose"], ordered["p_pos"], color="red")
ax.set_xlabel("Glucose (mg/dL)"); ax.set_ylabel("Observed class (0/1) and P(pos)")
plt.show()










TipStuck?





In R the probability of the event is the column predict(type = "prob") named after the level you want. In Python predict_proba returns one column per class, in the order given by the estimator’s classes_ attribute — print it before you choose an index.



Two features of this plot deserve a sentence each. The curve never reaches 0 or 1: at the lowest real glucose in the file, 57 mg/dL, the model still gives 0.044, and it will not tell you a patient is safe. And there are five points at glucose = 0, which is not a glucose a living patient has; the file codes some missing values as zeros, which Chapter 5 takes apart.

title: 14  Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve
section: 14.8 Task 4 — Which column did you take?
text:
14.8 Task 4 — Which column did you take?
Half of all logistic regression errors are taking the probability of the wrong class. There is a check for it, and the reason the check works is worth knowing: a logistic regression with an intercept, scored on the rows it was fitted to, produces fitted probabilities whose mean equals the observed prevalence exactly. Take the other column and you get one minus it.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
p_pos <- predict(fit_glucose, new_data = diabetes, type = "prob")$______
check_probabilities(p_pos, prevalence = mean(diabetes$diabetes == "pos"))




# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
print("classes_:", fit_glucose.classes_)
p_pos = fit_glucose.predict_proba(X)[:, ______]
check_probabilities(p_pos, prevalence=float(y.mean()))




Run it deliberately wrong once — take .pred_neg, or column 0 — and read what the check says. A check you have never seen fail is a check you do not trust.
crumbs: 14  Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve

title: 14  Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve
section: 14.9 The result that should bother you
text:
14.9 The result that should bother you
The original course notes for this material relevel the outcome so that pos comes first, on the reasonable grounds that pos is the event of interest. Do that, and the coefficient on glucose becomes negative, while the predicted probability of diabetes for every patient stays exactly the same.

library(forcats)
relevelled <- diabetes |> mutate(diabetes = fct_relevel(diabetes, "pos"))
fit_relevelled <- logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm") |>
  fit(diabetes ~ glucose, data = relevelled)

round(c(original   = coef(fit_glucose$fit)[["glucose"]],
        relevelled = coef(fit_relevelled$fit)[["glucose"]]), 5)

#>   original relevelled 
#>    0.03549   -0.03549

p_orig <- predict(fit_glucose,    new_data = diabetes,   type = "prob")$.pred_pos
p_relv <- predict(fit_relevelled, new_data = relevelled, type = "prob")$.pred_pos
max(abs(p_orig - p_relv))

#> [1] 1.110223e-15



glm() models the probability of the last level of the factor. With levels neg, pos it models pos, so the coefficient is +0.0355: more glucose, more diabetes. Relevel, and the last level is neg, so the same engine now models the probability of not having diabetes and reports −0.0355.
parsnip knows this. It asks the engine for its own event, then returns both columns correctly labelled, which is why .pred_pos is identical to fifteen decimal places either way.
So the coefficient’s sign and the column’s name follow two different conventions, and the published page that made this change kept a sentence underneath saying the model was \(\operatorname{logit}(P(\text{pos})) = \beta_0
+ \beta_1 x\). With pos relevelled first, that sentence was false and the plot above it was right.

The transferable rule: never read a sign off a coefficient without checking which class the engine thinks it is modelling. The cheap way to check is the one you already have — predict for a patient with a high glucose and see which direction the probability went.

title: 14  Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve
section: 14.10 Reflection
text:
14.10 Reflection

The odds ratio is constant and the probability difference is not. Which of the two would you put in a patient-facing leaflet, and what would you have to add to make it honest?
This model has an accuracy you have not computed and a probability for every patient that you have. Which of those two would change if the study had recruited twice as many pos patients, and why does that matter for a model fitted on a case-control sample?

title: 14  Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve
section: 14.11 Stretch
text:
14.11 Stretch






NoteStretch 1 — Where is the curve steepest?



Find the glucose value at which the predicted probability is 0.5, from the two coefficients alone: it is \(-\beta_0/\beta_1\). Ours is about 144 mg/dL. This is the point at which the model is least sure, and — as Chapter 15 will show — it is also exactly what you are choosing when you choose a threshold of 0.5.








NoteStretch 2 — Add a predictor, and watch the coefficient move



Refit with diabetes ~ glucose + mass + age. The glucose coefficient changes a little (0.0355 to about 0.0328) and the intercept moves a long way (−5.10 to about −6.74). Explain why the second of those is arithmetic rather than news, and what the first one would have to look like before you called glucose confounded by age.

title: 14  Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve
section: 14.12 What you can and cannot now claim
text:
14.12 What you can and cannot now claim
Can: that for a patient drawn from this population, the model gives a probability of diabetes, and that you can produce and interpret that probability on all three scales.
Cannot: that any patient has diabetes. The model has not said so and cannot: a probability is not a decision, and nothing in the fitting procedure knows what it costs to be wrong in either direction. Turning 0.302 into a yes or a no is a separate act with separate consequences, and it is Chapter 15.
crumbs: 14  Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve

title: 15  Exercise 4.3 — Choosing a threshold
text: 15.1 Objectives

title: 15  Exercise 4.3 — Choosing a threshold
text:
Turn predicted probabilities into predicted classes at a stated threshold, and build the confusion table that results.
Say what moving the threshold from 0.5 to 0.3 buys and what it costs, in patients rather than in percentages.
Choose a threshold from a stated cost ratio, and defend the choice against the threshold that maximises accuracy.

title: 15  Exercise 4.3 — Choosing a threshold
section: 15.2 Why this, here
text:
15.2 Why this, here
Chapter 14 ended with a probability of 0.302 for a patient with a glucose of 120. No clinic can act on 0.302. Somebody has to decide whether that patient is investigated further, and that decision needs a cut-off.
The cut-off is not part of the model. Nothing in the fitting procedure chose 0.5, no diagnostic accuracy study supports it, and the software offers it as a default only because it has to offer something. Choosing it properly requires one piece of information the data does not contain: what it costs to be wrong in each of the two directions. In diabetes screening those costs are not remotely equal — a missed diagnosis is years of untreated hyperglycaemia, a false alarm is a fasting glucose test and a worried afternoon — and the whole of this exercise follows from that asymmetry.

title: 15  Exercise 4.3 — Choosing a threshold
section: 15.3 Fit on the training rows, predict on the held-out ones
text:
15.3 Fit on the training rows, predict on the held-out ones
Same split as Chapter 13: every fifth row held back, so that the two languages are working on the same 153 patients. This time we are making a claim about unseen patients, so the split is doing real work.

RPython



library(readr); library(dplyr); library(tidymodels)

diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

test_rows <- seq(5, nrow(diabetes), by = 5)
train <- diabetes[-test_rows, ]
test  <- diabetes[ test_rows, ]

15.4 A threshold is a rule, and a rule has consequences

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(preds, aes(x = glucose, y = .pred_pos, colour = diabetes)) +

Everything above a line is called positive, everything below it negative. With one predictor the picture is unusually honest: a probability threshold is a glucose cut-off, and these three are 119, 142 and 165 mg/dL. Any colour above a line that is not the positive class is a false alarm; any positive-class point below it is a missed diagnosis.

15.5 Task 1 — Three thresholds, three confusion tables
Count the four cells of the confusion table at 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7, and turn them into sensitivity, specificity and positive predictive value. Do it by counting first: the packaged functions come in the next section, and they are much easier to misuse than to use.

counts <- function(threshold) {
  called_pos <- preds$.pred_pos >= ______
  truly_pos  <- preds$diabetes == "pos"

         TP = sum(called_pos & truly_pos),
         FP = sum(called_pos & !truly_pos),
         FN = sum(!called_pos & ______),
         TN = sum(!called_pos & !truly_pos))
}

bind_rows(lapply(c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7), counts)) |>
  mutate(sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN),
         specificity = TN / (TN + FP),
         ppv         = TP / (TP + FP),
         accuracy    = (TP + TN) / nrow(preds))

section: 15.6 The packaged version, and the trap in it
text:
15.6 The packaged version, and the trap in it
Both languages ship a confusion-matrix function, and both have a convention about which class counts as the event. Getting it wrong silently swaps your sensitivity and your specificity.

RPython



preds_0.5 <- preds |>
  mutate(predicted = factor(if_else(.pred_pos >= 0.5, "pos", "neg"),
                            levels = c("neg", "pos")))

conf_mat(preds_0.5, truth = diabetes, estimate = predicted)

#>           Truth
#> Prediction neg pos
#>        neg  83  30
#>        pos  15  25

c(default      = sens(preds_0.5, truth = diabetes, estimate = predicted)$.estimate,
  event_second = sens(preds_0.5, truth = diabetes, estimate = predicted,
                      event_level = "second")$.estimate)

#>      default event_second 
#>    0.8469388    0.4545455





from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, recall_score

print(confusion_matrix(y_test, (p_pos >= 0.5).astype(int), labels=[0, 1]))

#> [[83 15]
#>  [30 25]]

{"pos_label=1": round(recall_score(y_test, (p_pos >= 0.5).astype(int)), 3),
 "pos_label=0": round(recall_score(y_test, (p_pos >= 0.5).astype(int), pos_label=0), 3)}

#> {'pos_label=1': 0.455, 'pos_label=0': 0.847}





yardstick treats the first factor level as the event, and our levels are neg, pos, so its default sensitivity of 0.847 is the specificity of the thing you care about. event_level = "second" recovers 0.455. scikit-learn makes the same decision with pos_label, which defaults to 1 and therefore happens to be right here — but only because we coded the outcome as 0/1 in that order.
The original course notes for this material converted the outcome to a 0/1 factor before calling conf_mat(), which made "0" the first level and the event. The table they printed was a correct table of the wrong event. It is a one-word fault, it does not raise an error, and the numbers it produces are plausible — which is the whole problem.

text:
15.7 Task 2 — Put a price on the two errors
A missed diagnosis is not a false alarm. For this exercise, take a missed case to cost five times what a false alarm costs — the ratio is a decision for a service, not a statistician, and Task 3 asks you to argue with it.
Compute the total cost over a grid of thresholds, find the cheapest one, and compare it with two strategies that use no model at all: investigate everybody, and investigate nobody.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
cost_of <- function(threshold, cost_fn = 5, cost_fp = 1) {
  called_pos <- preds$.pred_pos >= threshold
  truly_pos  <- preds$diabetes == "pos"
  cost_fn * sum(______ & truly_pos) + cost_fp * sum(called_pos & !truly_pos)
}

grid <- tibble(threshold = seq(0.01, 0.99, by = 0.01)) |>
  mutate(cost = sapply(threshold, cost_of))

best <- grid |> slice_min(cost, n = 1)
c(best_threshold = best$threshold, best_cost = best$cost,
  cost_at_0.5    = cost_of(0.5),
  investigate_everyone = cost_of(______),
  investigate_nobody   = cost_of(1.01))







TipStuck?





“Investigate everybody” is not a special case needing its own code: it is the rule you get from a threshold low enough that every predicted probability clears it. The lowest probability in the test set is 0.078.






# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
truly_pos = y_test.to_numpy() == 1

def cost_of(threshold, cost_fn=5, cost_fp=1):
    called_pos = p_pos >= threshold
    return cost_fn * (______ & truly_pos).sum() + cost_fp * (called_pos & ~truly_pos).sum()

grid = np.round(np.arange(0.01, 1.00, 0.01), 2)
costs = np.array([cost_of(t) for t in grid])

{"best_threshold": float(grid[costs.argmin()]), "best_cost": int(costs.min()),

 "investigate_everyone": int(cost_of(______)), "investigate_nobody": int(cost_of(1.01))}

title: 15  Exercise 4.3 — Choosing a threshold
section: 15.8 The result that should bother you
text:
15.8 The result that should bother you
The default threshold is not merely suboptimal here. It is beaten by a policy with no model in it.

At 0.5 the model’s accuracy is 0.706, against 0.641 for always saying neg. Six and a half percentage points for three decades of diabetes research, and a student reporting only accuracy would call that a working classifier.
At 0.5 the same model misses 30 of 55 cases. Those two sentences describe the same 153 patients. Accuracy is high because the model is good at the common class, and the common class is the one nobody is screening for.
Price the errors at 5:1 and the arithmetic turns hostile. The default threshold costs 165. Investigating every one of the 153 patients costs 98, because it incurs 98 false alarms and no missed cases. The model as deployed at its default is two-thirds worse than a policy that ignores it.

The model is not useless: at its cost-minimising threshold of 0.17 it costs 74, about a quarter less than investigating everybody. But that is the honest size of the win, it arrives only once somebody states the cost ratio, and it is invisible at 0.5.






NoteWhere 0.17 comes from



For a known cost ratio the optimal threshold is \(\text{cost}_{FP} / (\text{cost}_{FP} + \text{cost}_{FN})\) — here \(1/(1+5) = 0.167\) — whenever the predicted probabilities are well calibrated. Our grid finds 0.17 empirically on 153 patients, which is agreement to the nearest grid point and partly luck. The theoretical result is the thing to remember; the grid is what you run when you do not trust the calibration, which is most of the time.

}

                      sum(preds$.pred_pos >= t)

check_metric_range(sens_at(chosen), 0.80, 1.00, "sensitivity at the chosen threshold")

import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *

def sens_at(t):
    return ((p_pos >= t) & truly_pos).sum() / truly_pos.sum()

def ppv_at(t):
    return ((p_pos >= t) & truly_pos).sum() / (p_pos >= t).sum()

candidates = np.round(np.arange(0.01, 1.00, 0.01), 2)
chosen = max(t for t in candidates if sens_at(t) >= ______)

The answer is 0.28, which catches 44 of the 55 cases and raises 43 false alarms. Its positive predictive value is 0.506: half the people this rule sends for investigation do not have diabetes, and its accuracy, 0.647, is almost exactly the do-nothing baseline. A service can accept that — screening programmes routinely do — but only if someone has said so out loud. Write the two sentences before you look at the next section.

15.10 Reflection

Sensitivity rose from 0.455 to 0.800 and accuracy fell from 0.706 to 0.647. Explain to a sceptical colleague why that is an improvement, without using the word “cost”.
Everything here was computed on 153 patients with the prevalence this file happens to have. Name one thing that changes about your chosen threshold if the model is deployed in a population where diabetes is half as common, and say which of the four numbers in the confusion table move first.

section: 15.11 Stretch
text:
15.11 Stretch






NoteStretch 1 — All the thresholds at once



Plot sensitivity against 1 − specificity across the whole grid. You have just drawn a ROC curve by hand, and the area under it is the one classification summary that does not depend on the threshold — which is a virtue and a vice. Chapter 18 is the full treatment; arriving there having built the curve from counts is worth an hour of slides.








NoteStretch 2 — Choose the threshold honestly



Split the 615 training rows again into fit and validation parts, choose the threshold on the validation part, and only then report its cost on the test set. Does the cost go up? It usually does, and the gap is the price of having chosen the threshold on the data you then reported.








NoteStretch 3 — Does a better model move the threshold?



Refit with diabetes ~ glucose + mass + age and repeat Task 2. The cost at the best threshold falls; ask whether the best threshold itself moved, and whether you would have predicted the direction.

title: 15  Exercise 4.3 — Choosing a threshold
section: 15.12 What you can and cannot now claim
text:
15.12 What you can and cannot now claim
Can: that at a stated threshold, on 153 held-out patients, this model finds a stated fraction of the diabetes in them at a stated false-alarm rate — and that you can produce the threshold a stated cost ratio implies.
Cannot: that any of these thresholds is right for a real service. The cost ratio was invented for the exercise, the prevalence is this file’s, the probabilities have not been checked for calibration, and the threshold was chosen on the same rows it was scored on. Each of those is a day of its own, and Chapter 18 is the next one.

title: 16  Exercise 4.4 — Is a predicted 0.7 worth 0.7?
section: 16.2 Why this, here
text:
16.2 Why this, here
Chapter 15 chose a threshold of 0.17 from a cost ratio of five to one, and the arithmetic behind that choice assumed something it never checked: that a predicted probability of 0.17 belongs to a group of patients of whom about 17% really do have diabetes. If the probabilities are on a different scale from the events, the threshold is still a number but it is no longer the number the cost ratio implies.
That assumption has a name. A model is calibrated when, among the patients it gives probability \(q\), the long-run proportion with the outcome is \(q\). Calibration is a property of the probabilities themselves, and it is not measured by anything Day 4 has computed so far: accuracy, sensitivity and specificity all throw the probability away at the threshold and look only at the classes that come out.






NoteOne number borrowed from Day 5



Task 3 needs the area under the ROC curve, which is Chapter 18 and has not been taught yet. You need only one fact about it here: AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen positive patient is given a higher score than a randomly chosen negative one. It is a statement about order and nothing else. That is the whole point of Task 3, and you can take the number on trust until Day 5 explains it.

text:
16.3 Worked example — calibration in the large, and where it stops holding
Same model and same split as Chapter 15: diabetes ~ glucose, fitted to 615 patients, scored on the 153 held back.

RPython



library(readr); library(dplyr); library(tidymodels)

diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

test_rows <- seq(5, nrow(diabetes), by = 5)
train <- diabetes[-test_rows, ]
test  <- diabetes[ test_rows, ]

fit <- logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm") |> fit(diabetes ~ glucose, data = train)

p_train <- predict(fit, train, type = "prob")$.pred_pos
p_logit <- predict(fit, test,  type = "prob")$.pred_pos

source("checks/checks.R")
cat("on the training rows\n")

#> on the training rows

check_probabilities(p_train, prevalence = mean(train$diabetes == "pos"))

#> [ok]  every value is a probability between 0 and 1  (range 0.005 to 0.894)
#> [ok]  the mean predicted probability matches the observed prevalence  (mean 0.366 vs prevalence 0.366)

cat("on the held-out rows\n")

#> on the held-out rows

check_probabilities(p_logit, prevalence = mean(test$diabetes == "pos"))

#> [ok]  every value is a probability between 0 and 1  (range 0.078 to 0.874)
#> [fix] the mean predicted probability matches the observed prevalence  (mean 0.386 vs prevalence 0.359)
#>        hint: a logistic regression with an intercept averages to the prevalence on its training rows; if yours averages to one minus that, you have taken the other probability column





import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
is_test = (diabetes.index + 1) % 5 == 0
train, test = diabetes[~is_test], diabetes[is_test]

y_train = (train["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)
y_test  = (test["diabetes"]  == "pos").astype(int)

fit = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf, max_iter=1000).fit(train[["glucose"]], y_train)
p_train = fit.predict_proba(train[["glucose"]])[:, 1]
p_logit = fit.predict_proba(test[["glucose"]])[:, 1]

import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
print("on the training rows")

#> on the training rows

check_probabilities(p_train, prevalence=float(y_train.mean()))

#> [ok]  every value is a probability between 0 and 1  (range 0.005 to 0.894)
#> [ok]  the mean predicted probability matches the observed prevalence  (mean 0.366 vs prevalence 0.366)

print("on the held-out rows")

#> on the held-out rows

check_probabilities(p_logit, prevalence=float(y_test.mean()))

#> [ok]  every value is a probability between 0 and 1  (range 0.078 to 0.874)
#> [fix] the mean predicted probability matches the observed prevalence  (mean 0.386 vs prevalence 0.359)
#>        hint: a logistic regression with an intercept averages to the prevalence on its training rows; if yours averages to one minus that, you have taken the other probability column





The first check passes to six decimal places and it could not have done anything else: Chapter 14 showed that a logistic regression with an intercept makes the mean of its fitted probabilities equal the observed prevalence, exactly, on the rows it was fitted to. That is an algebraic identity, not evidence.
The second check reports [fix]. The mean predicted probability on the held-out patients is 0.386, the prevalence among them is 0.359, and the gap of 0.027 is larger than the check’s tolerance of 0.02. Nothing is broken: the training prevalence is 0.366 and the test prevalence is 0.359, so the model is carrying the training rate onto a test set that happens to be slightly healthier. This is the weakest possible calibration claim — calibration in the large, one number against one number — and the model already misses it by two and a half percentage points on 153 patients.
A model can pass that test and still be useless, because it averages. A model that gave every patient 0.359 would pass it perfectly.

16.4 Task 1 — The calibration curve, before a package draws one
Split the predicted probabilities into five bins of width 0.2. In each bin, count the patients, average the predictions, and compute the proportion who actually had diabetes. A calibrated model puts those last two columns on top of each other.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")

calibration_table <- function(p, truth, n_bins = 5) {
  edges <- seq(0, 1, length.out = ______ + 1)
  tibble(bin      = cut(p, breaks = edges, include.lowest = TRUE),
         p        = p,
         observed = as.integer(truth == "pos")) |>
    group_by(bin, .drop = FALSE) |>
    summarise(n              = n(),
              mean_predicted = mean(p),
              observed_rate  = mean(______),
              .groups = "drop")
}

logit_cal <- calibration_table(p_logit, test$diabetes)
logit_cal

gap_logit <- max(abs(logit_cal$mean_predicted - logit_cal$observed_rate), na.rm = TRUE)
check_metric_range(gap_logit, 0, 0.35, "largest predicted-minus-observed gap")

import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *

def calibration_table(p, truth, n_bins=5):
    p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float)
    bin_id = np.minimum((p * ______).astype(int), n_bins - 1)
    out = pd.DataFrame({"bin": bin_id, "p": p, "observed": np.asarray(truth)})
    return (out.groupby("bin")
               .agg(n=("p", "size"), mean_predicted=("p", "mean"),
                    observed_rate=("______", "mean"))
               .reindex(range(n_bins)))

logit_cal = calibration_table(p_logit, y_test)
print(logit_cal.round(4))

gap_logit = (logit_cal["mean_predicted"] - logit_cal["observed_rate"]).abs().max()
check_metric_range(gap_logit, 0, 0.35, "largest predicted-minus-observed gap")

section: 16.5 Is that top bin a fault, or is it sixteen patients?
text:
16.5 Is that top bin a fault, or is it sixteen patients?
Before reading anything into a gap, ask what gap you would see from a model that was perfectly calibrated. We can answer that exactly, because we can generate outcomes from the model’s own probabilities and rebuild the table. This reuses the calibration_table() you wrote in Task 1, so run that cell first.

RPython



set.seed(1)
max_gap <- function(y) {
  tab <- calibration_table(p_logit, factor(ifelse(y == 1, "pos", "neg"),
                                           levels = c("neg", "pos")))
  max(abs(tab$mean_predicted - tab$observed_rate), na.rm = TRUE)
}
simulated <- replicate(2000, max_gap(rbinom(length(p_logit), 1, p_logit)))

round(c(observed      = max_gap(as.integer(test$diabetes == "pos")),
        sim_median    = median(simulated),
        sim_90th      = unname(quantile(simulated, 0.90)),
        p_value       = mean(simulated >= max_gap(as.integer(test$diabetes == "pos")))), 3)

#>   observed sim_median   sim_90th    p_value 
#>      0.217      0.126      0.217      0.116





rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

def max_gap(y):
    tab = calibration_table(p_logit, y)
    return float((tab["mean_predicted"] - tab["observed_rate"]).abs().max())

observed = max_gap(y_test.to_numpy())
simulated = np.array([max_gap(rng.binomial(1, p_logit)) for _ in range(2000)])

{"observed": round(observed, 3),
 "sim_median": round(float(np.median(simulated)), 3),
 "sim_90th": round(float(np.quantile(simulated, 0.90)), 3),
 "p_value": round(float((simulated >= observed).mean()), 3)}

#> {'observed': 0.217, 'sim_median': 0.126, 'sim_90th': 0.217, 'p_value': 0.117}





A perfectly calibrated model on 153 patients in five bins produces a largest gap of 0.126 on a typical run, and exceeds the 0.217 we measured in about 12% of runs. The curve is not evidence that this model is miscalibrated. It is mostly evidence that sixteen patients is not many, and it is the reason calibration plots in papers should carry the bin counts — which is why calibration_table() returns n first.

section: 16.6 Task 2 — A second model, on the same patients
text:
16.6 Task 2 — A second model, on the same patients
Chapter 20 grows 500 trees and averages their votes, and averages of bounded numbers are pulled towards the middle. The standard warning is that an untouched random forest is poorly calibrated: too timid near 0 and near 1. Fit the Day 5.4 specification to these training rows, build its calibration table, and draw both curves against the diagonal.
The forest sees all eight predictors and the logistic regression sees one, so this is not a fair comparison of accuracy. It is a comparison of the shape of two curves, which is what the plot is for.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
library(ggplot2)
source("checks/checks.R")

set.seed(123)
rf <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger", seed = 123) |>
  set_mode("classification") |>
  fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train)

p_rf <- predict(rf, test, type = "prob")$______
check_probabilities(p_rf, prevalence = mean(test$diabetes == "pos"))

curves <- bind_rows(
  calibration_table(p_logit, test$diabetes) |> mutate(model = "logistic, glucose only"),
  calibration_table(p_rf,    test$diabetes) |> mutate(model = "random forest, 8 predictors")
) |> filter(n > 0)

ggplot(curves, aes(x = mean_predicted, y = ______, colour = model)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(aes(size = n)) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Mean predicted probability in the bin",
       y = "Observed rate in the bin", colour = NULL, size = "patients")




# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *

rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=123).fit(
    train.drop(columns="diabetes"), y_train)
p_rf = rf.predict_proba(test.drop(columns="diabetes"))[:, ______]
check_probabilities(p_rf, prevalence=float(y_test.mean()))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 5))
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], linestyle="--", color="grey")
for p, label in [(p_logit, "logistic, glucose only"),
                 (p_rf, "random forest, 8 predictors")]:
    tab = calibration_table(p, y_test).dropna()
    ax.plot(tab["mean_predicted"], tab["______"], marker="o", label=label)
ax.set_xlabel("Mean predicted probability in the bin")
ax.set_ylabel("Observed rate in the bin")
ax.legend()
plt.show()










TipStuck?





The forest’s probability column has the same name as the logistic regression’s, because parsnip names it after the factor level; in Python predict_proba again returns one column per class in classes_ order. The second blank is the column of calibration_table() that holds what actually happened.



The warning does not come true here, and that is worth more than if it had. The forest’s probabilities reach both ends of the interval — 0.008 to 0.906 in R, 0.004 to 0.924 in Python — rather than huddling near the prevalence, its mean is 0.362 against a prevalence of 0.359 — it passes the check the logistic regression failed — and its largest bin gap is 0.19 in R and 0.30 in Python. Neither model is distinguishable from calibrated at this sample size, and the two languages disagree about which looks worse, which tells you how much signal there is in the comparison.
Pile-up towards the middle is real, but it is a property of small or heavily regularised ensembles. Five hundred unrestricted trees on 615 patients are confident enough to reach both ends.

title: 16  Exercise 4.4 — Is a predicted 0.7 worth 0.7?
section: 16.7 Task 3 — Same order, different numbers
text:
16.7 Task 3 — Same order, different numbers
Now break the probabilities on purpose, in a way no ranking metric can see. Shrink every prediction a third of the way towards 0.5:
\[q = 0.5 + \frac{p - 0.5}{3}.\]
This is strictly increasing in \(p\), so the patients come out in exactly the same order. Compute the AUC before and after, and the calibration table after.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
p_squashed <- 0.5 + (p_logit - 0.5) / ______

auc_raw      <- roc_auc_vec(test$diabetes, p_logit,     event_level = "second")
auc_squashed <- roc_auc_vec(test$diabetes, ______, event_level = "second")
check_matches(auc_squashed, auc_raw, tol = 1e-4, label = "AUC after squashing")

brier <- function(p) mean((p - as.integer(test$diabetes == "pos"))^2)
round(c(auc_raw = auc_raw, auc_squashed = auc_squashed,
        brier_raw = brier(p_logit), brier_squashed = brier(p_squashed)), 6)

check_probabilities(p_squashed, prevalence = mean(test$diabetes == "pos"))
calibration_table(p_squashed, test$diabetes)




# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, brier_score_loss
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *

p_squashed = 0.5 + (p_logit - 0.5) / ______

auc_raw      = roc_auc_score(y_test, p_logit)
auc_squashed = roc_auc_score(y_test, ______)
check_matches(auc_squashed, auc_raw, tol=1e-4, label="AUC after squashing")

print({"auc_raw": round(auc_raw, 6), "auc_squashed": round(auc_squashed, 6),
       "brier_raw": round(brier_score_loss(y_test, p_logit), 6),
       "brier_squashed": round(brier_score_loss(y_test, p_squashed), 6)})

check_probabilities(p_squashed, prevalence=float(y_test.mean()))
print(calibration_table(p_squashed, y_test).round(4))




The Brier score in that cell is the mean squared difference between the probability and the outcome coded 0 or 1. Unlike AUC it is a proper scoring rule: it is minimised by telling the truth, so it falls when the ranking improves and also when the numbers themselves get closer to the events.
crumbs: 16  Exercise 4.4 — Is a predicted 0.7 worth 0.7?

title: 16  Exercise 4.4 — Is a predicted 0.7 worth 0.7?
section: 16.8 The result that should bother you
text:
16.8 The result that should bother you
The squashed model and the original model are the same model. One is a one-line transformation of the other, and every patient keeps their position in the queue.

The AUC is 0.742022 before and 0.742022 after — identical to six decimal places, in both languages, because AUC counts pairs in the right order and the order did not change. A report that quotes only AUC cannot tell these two models apart, and most published model reports quote only AUC.
The Brier score rises from 0.199 to 0.218, and the probabilities now span 0.359 to 0.625. Every patient is told something between “a bit more likely than not to be fine” and “not far off even odds”, which is a model with nothing to say.
Apply Chapter 15’ cost-minimising threshold of 0.17 to each. The original probabilities send 123 of the 153 patients for investigation at a cost of 74. The squashed probabilities send all 153, at a cost of 98 — exactly the cost of ignoring the model and investigating everybody. The entire value Day 4.3 extracted from this model has been destroyed by a transformation that AUC says never happened.


RPython



cost_of <- function(p, threshold, cost_fn = 5, cost_fp = 1) {
  called_pos <- p >= threshold
  truly_pos  <- test$diabetes == "pos"
  cost_fn * sum(!called_pos & truly_pos) + cost_fp * sum(called_pos & !truly_pos)
}
p_squashed <- 0.5 + (p_logit - 0.5) / 3

for (threshold in c(0.17, 0.5)) {
  print(rbind(
    raw      = c(threshold = threshold, n_investigated = sum(p_logit    >= threshold),
                 cost = cost_of(p_logit,    threshold)),
    squashed = c(threshold = threshold, n_investigated = sum(p_squashed >= threshold),
                 cost = cost_of(p_squashed, threshold))))
}

#>          threshold n_investigated cost
#> raw           0.17            123   74
#> squashed      0.17            153   98
#>          threshold n_investigated cost
#> raw            0.5             40  165
#> squashed       0.5             40  165





truly_pos = y_test.to_numpy() == 1
p_squashed = 0.5 + (p_logit - 0.5) / 3

def cost_of(p, threshold, cost_fn=5, cost_fp=1):
    called_pos = p >= threshold
    return int(cost_fn * (~called_pos & truly_pos).sum()
               + cost_fp * (called_pos & ~truly_pos).sum())

pd.DataFrame([
    dict(model=name, threshold=t, n_investigated=int((p >= t).sum()), cost=cost_of(p, t))
    for t in (0.17, 0.5)
    for name, p in [("raw", p_logit), ("squashed", p_squashed)]
])

#>       model  threshold  n_investigated  cost
#> 0       raw       0.17             123    74
#> 1  squashed       0.17             153    98
#> 2       raw       0.50              40   165
#> 3  squashed       0.50              40   165





The sting is in the two rows for 0.5. At that threshold the two models are indistinguishable — both call 40 patients positive and both cost 165 — because 0.5 is the one point this transformation leaves alone. A team that had never moved off the default would have found nothing wrong, and would have been right that nothing was wrong for them. Calibration starts to matter the moment the threshold stops being arbitrary.

title: 16  Exercise 4.4 — Is a predicted 0.7 worth 0.7?
section: 16.9 Reflection
text:
16.9 Reflection

AUC did not move and the Brier score did. Write the one-sentence rule you would give a colleague for when AUC alone is an adequate summary of a clinical prediction model, and when it is not.
The noise simulation said we cannot tell this model from a calibrated one on 153 patients. How many patients would you want before you were willing to publish a calibration curve with five bins, and what would you report alongside it if you could not get them?
crumbs: 16  Exercise 4.4 — Is a predicted 0.7 worth 0.7?

title: 16  Exercise 4.4 — Is a predicted 0.7 worth 0.7?
section: 16.10 Stretch
text:
16.10 Stretch






NoteStretch 1 — Fix the imbalance, break the probabilities



The booklet has quoted a prevalence near 36% since Chapter 4 and never resampled it. Try it: keep all 225 pos training patients, draw an equal number of neg at random, refit diabetes ~ glucose on the balanced 450, and predict the same 153 test patients.
Nothing happens to the ranking. With one predictor the fitted probability is a monotone function of glucose whichever rows you fitted on, so the test AUC comes back as 0.742022 again, to the last digit. Everything happens to the scale: the mean predicted probability rises from 0.386 to about 0.49, against a prevalence of 0.359, and the Brier score rises from 0.199 to about 0.212. Chapter 15’ threshold of 0.17 now costs 94 or 95 instead of 74, because on the balanced model 0.17 is a glucose of about 83 rather than about 100 and almost every patient clears it.
The model is not worse. It is answering a different question — the risk in a population where diabetes is half as common as it is here is not the risk in this one — and the threshold was measured on the old scale. Re-minimising the cost on the new probabilities finds 0.26 or 0.27, and the cost there is 74 again: the same decisions, relabelled. Ask what you would have had to know to spot this if someone handed you only the resampled model and its AUC.








NoteStretch 2 — Put it back



Fit a logistic regression of the outcome on the log-odds of the squashed predictions, using the test set’s own outcomes, and look at the slope. This is Platt scaling, and on a monotone distortion it undoes the damage almost exactly. Then say why doing it on the test set, as you just did, is not allowed, and what you would have had to hold back at the start to do it properly.

title: 16  Exercise 4.4 — Is a predicted 0.7 worth 0.7?
section: 16.11 What you can and cannot now claim
text:
16.11 What you can and cannot now claim
Can: that you can build and read a calibration table for a set of predicted probabilities, that you can say whether its wobbles are larger than the sampling noise of the test set, and that you know one metric which notices a distortion that AUC cannot.
Cannot: that this model is calibrated. The honest finding is weaker and more useful: on 153 held-out patients it is not detectably miscalibrated, which is a statement about the test set at least as much as about the model. Nor can you claim that calibration survives deployment — Chapter 3’s covariate shift moves the case mix, and a model calibrated in development is routinely not calibrated in the clinic.
