title: 23  Exercise 9.2 — SHAP, one patient at a time
section: 23.8 A fairer comparison — logistic regression coefficients
text:
23.8 A fairer comparison — logistic regression coefficients
The usual next slide puts SHAP next to the coefficients of a logistic regression and invites you to compare the two rankings. Done naively that comparison is meaningless, and it is worth seeing why.

lr = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, solver="liblinear",
                        random_state=123).fit(X_train, y_train)
print("logistic regression test AUC", round(roc_auc_score(y_test, lr.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]), 3))

#> logistic regression test AUC 0.762

coef = pd.Series(lr.coef_[0], index=X.columns)
print("\nraw coefficients, log-odds per unit:")

#> 
#> raw coefficients, log-odds per unit:

print(coef.round(3))

#> pregnant    0.096
#> glucose     0.029
#> pressure   -0.014
#> triceps     0.002
#> insulin     0.000
#> mass        0.015
#> pedigree    0.519
#> age        -0.004
#> noise      -0.031
#> dtype: float64


The largest coefficient by a factor of five belongs to pedigree. That is an artefact of the units: pedigree runs from about 0.08 to 2.4, while glucose runs to 199, so a coefficient “per unit” means something a hundred times smaller for glucose. Multiply each coefficient by the training standard deviation of its variable and you have the change in log-odds per standard deviation, which is comparable across variables.

coef_sd = (coef * X_train.std()).sort_values()
print(coef_sd.round(3))

#> pressure   -0.301
#> age        -0.052
#> noise      -0.030
#> triceps     0.030
#> insulin     0.053
#> mass        0.126
#> pedigree    0.192
#> pregnant    0.374
#> glucose     0.950
#> dtype: float64

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.5))
coef_sd.plot(kind="barh", ax=ax, color="mediumseagreen")
ax.axvline(0, color="grey", linewidth=1)
ax.set_xlabel("change in log-odds per 1 SD")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()








On that scale glucose is the largest by a wide margin and pedigree has dropped to fourth. The ranking reversed because of a unit conversion, not because of anything in the data.
Two further things are worth noticing. The logistic regression’s test AUC is about the same as the forest’s: the black box bought you nothing here, which is worth remembering before you spend a day explaining it. And pressure gets a substantial negative standardised coefficient while the forest gives it almost no SHAP at all — two models of the same data disagreeing about a variable, which is a fact about the models.

title: 23  Exercise 9.2 — SHAP, one patient at a time
section: 23.9 Task 3 — Put the four measures side by side
text:
23.9 Task 3 — Put the four measures side by side
Build one table with a column per method, each scaled to its own maximum so the columns are on a common footing, and read off where the control sits in each.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

perm = pd.Series(permutation_importance(
    rf, X_test, y_test, n_repeats=20, random_state=123,
    scoring="roc_auc").importances_mean, index=X.columns)

comparison = pd.DataFrame({
    "impurity":    pd.Series(rf.feature_importances_, index=X.columns),
    "permutation": perm,
    "mean |SHAP|": pd.Series(np.abs(phi).mean(axis=0), index=X.columns),
    "|coef| per SD": ______,
})
comparison = comparison / comparison.______()
print(comparison.round(2).sort_values("mean |SHAP|", ascending=False))







TipStuck?





The fourth column is the standardised coefficients you just computed, without their signs — importance measures have no direction, so take the absolute value. Scaling a data frame by its column maxima is one method call.



Every column agrees that glucose is first. Below that they disagree about almost everything, and the noise row is between 0 and 0.37 depending on which method you happened to run.

title: 23  Exercise 9.2 — SHAP, one patient at a time
section: 23.10 The result that should bother you
text:
23.10 The result that should bother you
An explanation does not know whether the model is any good. Here is the same forest fitted to the same predictors with the outcome column shuffled, so that there is no relationship left to learn.

y_shuffled = np.random.default_rng(0).permutation(y_train.values)
rf_null = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=123).fit(X_train, y_shuffled)
print("test AUC of the shuffled-label forest:",
      round(roc_auc_score(y_test, rf_null.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]), 3))

#> test AUC of the shuffled-label forest: 0.467

phi_null = shap.TreeExplainer(rf_null).shap_values(X_test)[:, :, 1]
shap.summary_plot(phi_null, X_test, show=False, plot_size=(6.5, 4))
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()








The AUC is about 0.47 — worse than a coin toss. The beeswarm is still a beeswarm: variables are ranked, dots are coloured, one predictor leads the others by a clear margin. The contributions are about a third the size of the real model’s, which you would only notice by looking at the axis, and shap will not tell you.

SHAP explains the function the model computes. It has no access to the outcome, so it cannot know the function is worthless.
Therefore a SHAP plot is never evidence that a model works. The evidence that a model works is a held-out score against a baseline, and it has to come first.
And the ordering in a SHAP plot of a model that does not work is just the ordering of its overfitting.

title: 23  Exercise 9.2 — SHAP, one patient at a time
section: 23.13 What you can and cannot now claim
text:
23.13 What you can and cannot now claim
Can: that for this forest, this patient’s prediction of 0.71 decomposes exactly into a base rate of 0.37 plus a set of contributions dominated by glucose; and that the same decomposition, done on a model that cannot predict anything, looks much the same.
Cannot: that glucose caused anything, that lowering it would lower the prediction for a future patient, or that the forest has found something about diabetes. The first of those needs a causal question asked properly; the others need an experiment. Chapter 24 asks the same questions in R, and adds the one plot that at least looks like an intervention — and shows why it is not one.

title: 24  Exercise 9.3 — The same questions in R, with DALEX
section: 24.2 Why this, here
text:
24.2 Why this, here
Chapter 22 and Chapter 23 were Python. The methods are not Python’s: DALEX gives you permutation importance, Shapley attributions, partial dependence and individual conditional expectation from one explainer object, wrapped around any model that can predict. This chapter answers the same questions in R, on the same data and the same control column, so you can see that the conclusions belong to the methods and not to the language. It also adds the one family of plot that Python’s shap does not give you, and that is the one with the sharpest assumption buried in it.
crumbs: 24  Exercise 9.3 — The same questions in R, with DALEX

title: 24  Exercise 9.3 — The same questions in R, with DALEX
section: 24.3 One explainer, any model
text:
24.3 One explainer, any model
DALEX works by wrapping the model in a uniform interface: the data, the true outcome, and a function that turns rows into predictions. Everything else is computed from that, which is why the same code works for a forest, a regression or something written by someone else entirely.

library(readr); library(dplyr); library(tidymodels)
library(DALEX); library(DALEXtra); library(vip); library(ggplot2)

set.seed(123)
dia <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")),
         noise    = round(rnorm(n()), 2))

split <- initial_split(dia, prop = 0.7, strata = diabetes)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

rf_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(recipe(diabetes ~ ., data = train) |>
               step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())) |>
  add_model(rand_forest(trees = 500, mtry = 3, min_n = 10) |>
              set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity", seed = 123) |>
              set_mode("classification"))

rf_fit <- fit(rf_wf, data = train)

explainer <- explain_tidymodels(
  rf_fit,
  data  = select(test, -diabetes),
  y     = as.numeric(test$diabetes == "pos"),
  label = "random forest",
  verbose = FALSE
)







WarningRead the y argument twice



diabetes is a factor, and as.numeric() on a factor returns the level codes — 1 and 2, not 0 and 1. Pass that to explain_tidymodels() and the explainer believes every patient has an outcome of at least 1 while the model predicts probabilities below 1, so every residual is positive and the mean residual is about 1. Nothing errors. The importance plot still draws. Compare with as.numeric(test$diabetes == "pos"), which gives the 0/1 the explainer expects.
The diagnostic is free: print the explainer with verbose = TRUE and read the residual line. If the mean residual is not near zero, the outcome is wrong.



# the free diagnostic: residuals should straddle zero
round(summary(explainer$residuals), 3)

#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>  -0.844  -0.291  -0.078   0.001   0.283   0.932
crumbs: 24  Exercise 9.3 — The same questions in R, with DALEX

title: 24  Exercise 9.3 — The same questions in R, with DALEX
section: 24.4 Task 1 — Global importance, and the control for the third time
text:
24.4 Task 1 — Global importance, and the control for the third time
model_parts() is permutation importance: it shuffles each variable B times and records the loss. For a classification task the default loss is one minus AUC, so a variable that matters has a higher dropout loss than the full model.

set.seed(123)
mp <- model_parts(explainer, B = 20)
plot(mp)








_full_model_ marks the intact loss and _baseline_ the loss of a model that predicts the mean, so the distance between them is all the AUC the forest has. Turn the losses into drops and run the control check.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")

losses <- as.data.frame(______) |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  summarise(loss = mean(dropout_loss), .groups = "drop")
full   <- losses$loss[losses$variable == "_full_model_"]
drops  <- setNames(losses$loss - ______, losses$variable)
drops  <- drops[!names(drops) %in% c("_baseline_", "_full_model_")]

round(sort(drops, decreasing = TRUE), 4)
check_noise_control(drops)







TipStuck?





The quantity you want is each variable’s mean loss minus the loss of the intact model, which is the row model_parts() labels _full_model_. The object to summarise is the one you just plotted.



The picture matches Python’s to the extent that you should expect: glucose far ahead, age second, everything else in an undifferentiated band, and the control inside that band at a few per cent of glucose.

section: 24.5 Partial dependence — the average patient who does not exist
text:
24.5 Partial dependence — the average patient who does not exist
A partial dependence profile asks: if I set this variable to \(v\) for every patient in the data, leaving all their other values alone, what does the model predict on average? Sweep \(v\) across the observed range and you get a curve.

pdp_glucose  <- model_profile(explainer, variable = "glucose",  type = "partial")
pdp_pedigree <- model_profile(explainer, variable = "pedigree", type = "partial")
plot(pdp_glucose, pdp_pedigree)








Glucose moves the average prediction from about 0.19 to about 0.74 across its range — a real and large effect. Pedigree moves it very little, and most of what movement there is sits at the sparse right-hand end of the variable.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
plot(pdp_glucose, geom = ______) +
  ggtitle("Ceteris paribus profiles for glucose, with the average")







TipStuck?





The argument is geom, and the value is named in the sentence above the cell. ?plot.model_profile lists the alternatives.



Describe the spread. Do all patients respond to glucose in the same way, and would you be happy to quote the average curve to someone asking about one patient?

text:
24.7 Local explanation — the same patient, a different algorithm
predict_parts(type = "shap") computes Shapley values by sampling orderings of the variables, rather than exploiting the tree structure as TreeExplainer does. It is slower and approximate, and it works for models that are not trees.

patient <- test[1, setdiff(names(test), "diabetes")]
patient

#> # A tibble: 1 × 9
#>   pregnant glucose pressure triceps insulin  mass pedigree   age noise
#>      <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1        8     129       84       0       0  27.6    0.828    44 -0.23

cat("predicted:", round(predict(explainer, patient), 3),
    " actual:", as.character(test$diabetes[1]), "\n")

#> predicted: 0.655  actual: pos

set.seed(123)
local_shap <- predict_parts(explainer, new_observation = patient,
                            type = "shap", B = 25)
plot(local_shap)








The bars are the same quantity as Chapter 23’s force plot, drawn differently and estimated by a different algorithm. The boxplots behind them are the spread across the 25 sampled orderings — a feature the Python plot does not show you, and a useful reminder that these contributions are estimates with uncertainty unless your model is a tree ensemble.

24.8 Task 3 — The forest’s own importance, for comparison
vip() reads the impurity importance the ranger engine stored while fitting. Plot it, and put it next to the permutation ranking from Task 1.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
imp <- vi(extract_fit_parsnip(______))
imp
check_noise_control(imp)







TipStuck?





vi() needs the model itself, not the workflow that contains it. extract_fit_parsnip() reaches inside a fitted workflow and hands you the parsnip fit.



Same disagreement as in Python, in the same direction: impurity puts the control fifth of nine at around 30% of glucose, permutation puts it in the noise band at a few per cent. Two measures, one model, one figure each, and only the second one is about prediction.

title: 24  Exercise 9.3 — The same questions in R, with DALEX
section: 24.9 The result that should bother you
text:
24.9 The result that should bother you
Ask for a partial dependence profile of insulin.

# the profile averages the model over the explainer's data, which is the test set
cat("rows with insulin recorded as 0:",
    sum(test$insulin == 0), "of", nrow(test), "\n")

#> rows with insulin recorded as 0: 130 of 231

cat("largest observed insulin:", max(test$insulin), "\n")

#> largest observed insulin: 846

plot(model_profile(explainer, variable = "insulin", type = "partial"))








It is a smooth, gently rising curve, and it is nonsense. Three steps.

More than half the rows the profile averages over record insulin as exactly zero, which is not a measurement — it is a missing value written as a number, the defect you met in Chapter 5. The curve’s left-hand end is the model’s behaviour on “not measured”, plotted as though it were a concentration.
The curve’s right-hand end sets insulin to its maximum for every patient, including the ones whose insulin was never measured and the ones for whom that combination of values is physiologically impossible. Partial dependence averages the model over rows that do not exist and could not exist.
So the curve is well defined as a property of the fitted function, and it is not an answer to “what happens if insulin rises”. That question is causal, and nothing on this page can answer it.

The same objection applies, more weakly, to every other partial dependence plot you will ever be shown. Variables are correlated; holding the others fixed while moving one walks you off the data.

24.10 Reflection

DALEX and shap gave the same patient’s explanation by different algorithms. What would you conclude if they had disagreed substantially, and what would you check first?
The partial dependence plot for glucose looks like a dose–response curve. Write the sentence that distinguishes what it shows from what a dose–response curve shows.
You have now explained this forest in two languages with four methods. What is the single piece of evidence that would most change your willingness to put it in front of a clinician — and is it on any of these pages?

section: 24.11 Stretch
text:
24.11 Stretch






NoteStretch 1 — Explain a model DALEX has never heard of



Fit a logistic regression with glm() and build an explainer for it with DALEX::explain(), passing your own predict_function. Put its model_parts() next to the forest’s. The point is not the comparison; it is that the explainer needed nothing from the model except the ability to predict.








NoteStretch 2 — Accumulated local effects



Re-draw the insulin profile with type = "accumulated". ALE profiles average the model’s local slope over the data that actually exists, rather than over a grid of invented rows. How much does the curve change, and does the change support or undermine the reading you gave in step 3 above?

title: 24  Exercise 9.3 — The same questions in R, with DALEX
section: 24.12 What you can and cannot now claim
text:
24.12 What you can and cannot now claim
Can: that this forest, explained in R by three methods, tells the same story as the Python explanations of Chapter 23 — glucose dominates, nothing else is clearly separated from the control, and the model’s own impurity importance disagrees with all of it.
Cannot: that any of this is evidence about diabetes. Every figure on this page is a description of a function that was fitted to 537 rows of one file. What that function has to do with patients is a question none of today’s tools can be made to answer.

title: 25  Exercise 9.4 — For whom is the model worst?
section: 25.2 Why this, here
text:
25.2 Why this, here
Chapter 22, Chapter 23 and Chapter 24 asked which variables the model used. None of them asked who the model works for. Every metric in this booklet — Chapter 18’ AUC, Chapter 15’ sensitivity, Chapter 20’s comparison table — has been computed on all 231 test rows at once, and a single number over 231 people is an average over people who are not interchangeable. Chapter 2 asked where the model is wrong. A service has to answer a harder version: for whom. This exercise splits the test set and asks that question, and then spends most of its time on whether the answer means anything.

title: 25  Exercise 9.4 — For whom is the model worst?
section: 25.3 Worked example — one model, scored on everyone
text:
25.3 Worked example — one model, scored on everyone
We audit the random forest of Chapter 20 rather than the logistic regression of Chapter 14, for one reason: it is the model Day 9 has spent all day explaining, and an equity audit in practice arrives after the explanation, on the model somebody is proposing to deploy. Nothing in the method depends on that choice — Stretch 1 repeats the whole page on the logistic regression, and the interesting question is whether the two models fail the same people.

RPython



library(tidymodels); library(readr); library(dplyr); library(ggplot2)

diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv") |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("pos", "neg")))

set.seed(123)
split <- initial_split(diabetes, prop = 0.7, strata = diabetes)
train <- training(split); test <- testing(split)

rf_fit <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger", seed = 123) |>
  set_mode("classification") |>
  fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train)

pred <- augment(rf_fit, test)

# every metric in one place, and the two counts that have to travel with them
metrics_in <- function(d) {
  tibble(n     = nrow(d),
         cases = sum(d$diabetes == "pos"),
         sens  = if (any(d$diabetes == "pos")) sens_vec(d$diabetes, d$.pred_class) else NA_real_,
         spec  = if (any(d$diabetes == "neg")) spec_vec(d$diabetes, d$.pred_class) else NA_real_,
         auc   = if (n_distinct(d$diabetes) == 2) roc_auc_vec(d$diabetes, d$.pred_pos) else NA_real_)
}

by_group <- function(d, col) {
  d |> group_by(group = .data[[col]]) |> group_modify(~ metrics_in(.x)) |> ungroup()
}

metrics_in(pred)

#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>       n cases  sens  spec   auc
#>   <int> <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1   231    84 0.536 0.850 0.824





import pandas as pd, numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import recall_score, roc_auc_score

diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
X = diabetes.drop(columns="diabetes")
y = (diabetes["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3,
                                          random_state=123, stratify=y)

rf_fit = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=123).fit(X_tr, y_tr)

pred = X_te.copy()
pred["truth"] = y_te
pred["pred"]  = rf_fit.predict(X_te)
pred["prob"]  = rf_fit.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]

# every metric in one place, and the two counts that have to travel with them
def metrics_in(d):
    t, yhat, p = d["truth"].values, d["pred"].values, d["prob"].values
    return pd.Series({
        "n": len(t), "cases": int(t.sum()),
        "sens": recall_score(t, yhat) if t.sum() else np.nan,
        "spec": recall_score(1 - t, 1 - yhat) if (1 - t).sum() else np.nan,
        "auc":  roc_auc_score(t, p) if 0 < t.sum() < len(t) else np.nan})

def by_group(d, col):
    return pd.DataFrame({g: metrics_in(sub)
                         for g, sub in d.groupby(col, observed=True)}).T

metrics_in(pred).round(3)

#> n        231.000
#> cases     84.000
#> sens       0.631
#> spec       0.748
#> auc        0.768
#> dtype: float64





One row, 231 patients, 84 of them with diabetes. R’s split gives a sensitivity of 0.54 and an AUC of 0.82; Python’s gives 0.63 and 0.77. That row is the only performance statement the booklet has made so far, and a commissioner reading it has no way to tell whether it describes everybody equally.






Notecases, not just n



metrics_in() returns two counts, and the second one is the one people forget. Sensitivity is computed only on the patients who have the disease, so a group of 63 women containing 8 cases gives you a sensitivity estimated from 8 observations, however reassuring the 63 looks in the table.

25.4 Task 1 — Split the test set, and report the gap
Cut the test set two ways — by age band and by number of pregnancies — and compute the three metrics inside each band. Report, for each grouping, the distance between the best and the worst group, with the group sizes beside it.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")

pred <- pred |>
  mutate(age_band  = cut(age, c(-Inf, 30, 40, 50, Inf), right = FALSE,
                         labels = c("21-29", "30-39", "40-49", "50+")),
         preg_band = ______(pregnant, c(-Inf, 1, 3, 6, Inf), right = FALSE,
                            labels = c("0", "1-2", "3-5", "6+")))

by_age  <- by_group(pred, ______)
by_preg <- by_group(pred, "preg_band")
by_age
by_preg

gap_sens <- max(by_age$sens) - ______(by_age$sens)
cat("age bands - gap in sensitivity:", round(gap_sens, 3),
    " specificity:", round(max(by_age$spec) - min(by_age$spec), 3),
    " AUC:",         round(max(by_age$auc)  - min(by_age$auc),  3), "\n")

check_metric_range(gap_sens, 0, 1, "sensitivity gap")

import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *

pred["age_band"]  = pd.cut(pred["age"], [0, 30, 40, 50, np.inf], right=False,
                           labels=["21-29", "30-39", "40-49", "50+"])
pred["preg_band"] = pd.______(pred["pregnant"], [0, 1, 3, 6, np.inf], right=False,
                              labels=["0", "1-2", "3-5", "6+"])

by_age  = by_group(pred, ______)
by_preg = by_group(pred, "preg_band")
print(by_age.round(3))
print(by_preg.round(3))

gap_sens = by_age["sens"].max() - by_age["sens"].______()
print("age bands - gap in sensitivity:", round(gap_sens, 3),
      " specificity:", round(by_age["spec"].max() - by_age["spec"].min(), 3),
      " AUC:",         round(by_age["auc"].max()  - by_age["auc"].min(),  3))

check_metric_range(gap_sens, 0, 1, "sensitivity gap")










TipStuck?





Both languages have one function that turns a numeric column into bands with labels you choose; in R it is base, in Python it lives in pandas. The gap is the range of a column, so max() and min() are all you need — and if your answer comes back as a missing value, one band had only one class in it, which check_metric_range() will tell you by failing.



The age table is the kind of table that gets into a slide deck. In R the 40–49 band has a sensitivity of 0.73 against 0.46 for the under-30s; in Python the over-50s sit at 0.46 against 0.82 for the 40–49s. Before reading anything into either, look at the n and cases columns.

title: 25  Exercise 9.4 — For whom is the model worst?
section: 25.5 Task 2 — How large a gap does chance produce?
text:
25.5 Task 2 — How large a gap does chance produce?
The honest question is not whether the groups differ. With four groups and 231 rows they will always differ. The question is whether they differ by more than they would if there were nothing to find.
Build the comparison the only way that needs no assumptions: shuffle the band labels among the test rows, so the groups keep their sizes and lose their meaning, recompute the gap, and do it a thousand times. That distribution is the noise floor.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")

set.seed(123)
null_gaps <- replicate(1000, {
  shuffled <- pred |> mutate(age_band = ______(age_band))
  g <- by_group(shuffled, "age_band")
  max(g$sens) - min(g$sens)
})

round(quantile(null_gaps, c(0.5, 0.95)), 3)
check_gap_vs_noise(______, null_gaps, "sensitivity gap across age bands")




# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *

rng = np.random.default_rng(123)
shuffled, null_gaps = pred.copy(), []
for _ in range(1000):
    shuffled["age_band"] = rng.______(pred["age_band"].values)
    g = by_group(shuffled, "age_band")
    null_gaps.append(g["sens"].max() - g["sens"].min())
null_gaps = np.array(null_gaps)

print(np.quantile(null_gaps, [0.5, 0.95]).round(3))
check_gap_vs_noise(______, null_gaps, "sensitivity gap across age bands")










TipStuck?





Shuffling a column is one function call: in R it is the same function you use to draw a sample, called with no size argument; in Python it is a method of the random generator you have already created. Nothing else in the loop changes.
A [fix] from check_gap_vs_noise() is a result, not a bug. Read its detail line before you touch the code.



check_gap_vs_noise() reports the observed gap, the median of the permuted gaps, their 95th centile and a permutation p-value. For the age bands it fails, in both languages: the gap in sensitivity across age is 0.28 in R against a median permuted gap of 0.28, and 0.36 in Python against a median of 0.26. Made-up groups of the same sizes produce a gap this large about half the time in R and about a fifth of the time in Python.

25.6 A second grouping, where the answer is different
Run the same two steps on the pregnancy bands. This is a worked example, not a task: the code is Task 1’s and Task 2’s with one column name changed, so it is written out here in full.

  mutate(preg_band = cut(pregnant, c(-Inf, 1, 3, 6, Inf), right = FALSE,
                         labels = c("0", "1-2", "3-5", "6+")))

by_preg

  labs(x = "sensitivity gap between four groups of the same sizes, labels shuffled",
       y = "permutations",
       title = "The noise floor, and the gap we observed (vertical line)")

title: 25  Exercise 9.4 — For whom is the model worst?
section: 25.7 Task 3 — Put an interval on every group
text:
25.7 Task 3 — Put an interval on every group
A p-value for the gap does not tell a service how good the model is for the over-50s. For that you need an interval around each group’s own estimate. Resample the rows within a band, with replacement, recompute sensitivity, and take the 2.5th and 97.5th centiles.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
boot_sens <- function(d, B = 1000) {
  v <- replicate(B, {
    i <- sample(nrow(d), replace = ______)
    if (any(d$diabetes[i] == "pos")) sens_vec(d$diabetes[i], d$.pred_class[i]) else NA_real_
  })
  quantile(v, c(0.025, ______), na.rm = TRUE)
}

set.seed(123)
intervals <- lapply(levels(pred$age_band), function(g) {
  d  <- dplyr::filter(pred, age_band == g)
  ci <- boot_sens(d)
  tibble(group = g, n = nrow(d), cases = sum(d$diabetes == "pos"),
         sens  = sens_vec(d$diabetes, d$.pred_class),
         lo = ci[[1]], hi = ci[[2]], width = ci[[2]] - ci[[1]])
}) |> bind_rows()
intervals

cat("widest interval:", intervals$group[which.max(intervals$width)],
    "| smallest band:", intervals$group[which.min(intervals$n)],
    "| lowest AUC:",    as.character(by_age$group[which.min(by_age$auc)]), "\n")




# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
def boot_sens(d, rng, B=1000):
    t, yhat = d["truth"].values, d["pred"].values
    v = [recall_score(t[i], yhat[i]) if t[i].sum() else np.nan
         for i in (rng.integers(0, len(d), ______) for _ in range(B))]
    return np.nanquantile(v, [0.025, ______])

rng = np.random.default_rng(123)
rows = []
for g, d in pred.groupby("age_band", observed=True):
    lo, hi = boot_sens(d, rng)
    rows.append({"group": g, "n": len(d), "cases": int(d["truth"].sum()),
                 "sens": recall_score(d["truth"], d["pred"]),
                 "lo": lo, "hi": hi, "width": hi - lo})
intervals = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(intervals.round(3))

print("widest interval:", intervals.loc[intervals["width"].idxmax(), "group"],
      "| smallest band:", intervals.loc[intervals["n"].idxmin(), "group"],
      "| lowest AUC:",    by_age["auc"].idxmin())










TipStuck?





A bootstrap resample is the same size as the group it came from, drawn with replacement — that is the whole idea, and it is one argument in R and one argument in Python. The upper centile is whatever makes the interval symmetric around 95%.

title: 25  Exercise 9.4 — For whom is the model worst?
section: 25.8 The result that should bother you
text:
25.8 The result that should bother you
The over-50s are the worst-served group in this test set. In R their AUC of 0.73 is the lowest of the four bands; in Python their AUC of 0.45 is the lowest of the four and below chance, which would mean the forest is worse than a coin for women over 50. They are also the band a service would most want to get right.
Three steps.

The over-50s band has 19 rows in R and 23 in Python, of which 11 are cases in both. It is the smallest band, it has the widest bootstrap interval of the four — 0.33 to 0.90 in R, 0.17 to 0.75 in Python — and the width of that interval, around 0.57 to 0.58, is larger than the entire gap between the best and worst band that we set out to interpret. The smallest group gets the most extreme point estimate because it has the fewest cases to average over, and the same thinness is what makes the estimate extreme and what makes it uncertain.
The direction is not stable either. The same band, the same model specification, the same seed: in R the over-50s have a sensitivity of 0.64, above the overall 0.54, and in Python 0.46, below the overall 0.63. The only difference between the two is which rows landed in the test set. A worst-served group that changes places when you reshuffle the split is a property of the split.
Permuting the labels says the same thing without any of the interpretation. Four made-up age bands of the same sizes produce a sensitivity gap of 0.28 or more in half of a thousand permutations, and the observed gap is 0.28. A difference smaller than the noise floor is not a finding, and ranking the bands by sensitivity is then an elaborate way of ranking them by size.

The pregnancy grouping is the useful counter-case, and it is only half a counter-case. That gap does clear the floor (p = 0.03 in R, p = 0.01 in Python), so something there is not chance. Then look at which band is driving it: the women with one or two pregnancies, sensitivity 0.25 in R and 0.17 in Python — estimated from 8 cases and 6 cases respectively, inside a group of 63 and 57 rows. Repeat Task 3 on the pregnancy bands and that band’s interval runs from 0.00 upwards. So even the gap that survives the permutation test rests on single-digit event counts, and we have looked at six gaps on this page — two groupings by three metrics — while testing two of them. A p-value of 0.03 is not a licence when the search was that wide.

title: 25  Exercise 9.4 — For whom is the model worst?
section: 25.9 What this cannot be evidence of
text:
25.9 What this cannot be evidence of






ImportantThe method is real; the finding is not



A subgroup gap measured on 231 test rows of a teaching extract is not evidence about any service. The smallest age band here holds eleven cases — few enough that a gap of the size you are about to find can be produced by chance alone — and no sentence of the form “the model under-serves group X” can be carried out of this chapter.
That is not a reason to skip the exercise; it is the exercise. Someone auditing a deployed model for equity has to be able to tell a disparity from an artefact of the data they were handed, and the only way to practise is on data where you already know the answer. What you would need to make a real claim is nameable: data from the service you are auditing, with the subgroup actually recorded rather than inferred; a list of subgroups written down before anyone looks at a metric; and enough cases in each of them — events, not rows — that the interval is narrower than the difference you would act on. On this page the third condition fails by a factor of several for every band.

title: 25  Exercise 9.4 — For whom is the model worst?
section: 25.10 Reflection
text:
25.10 Reflection

Your service wants a dashboard with one sensitivity per age band. Write the sentence you would put under the table so that a reader cannot misread a small group as a failing one. It should be a sentence, not a number.
Where does the list of subgroups come from? You cannot search the data for the grouping with the largest gap and then report that gap — explain why not, and say who should decide the list instead.
Suppose the over-50s disparity were real. Name two responses a service could make that are not “retrain the model”, and say what evidence would tell you which to choose.

title: 25  Exercise 9.4 — For whom is the model worst?
section: 25.11 Stretch
text:
25.11 Stretch






NoteStretch 1 — Do the two models fail the same people?



Repeat the whole page on the logistic regression of Chapter 14, fitted to the same training rows. Put its subgroup table next to the forest’s. If the two models disagree about which band is worst served, what does that tell you about the disparity — and what would it take for them to agree for the right reason rather than by chance?








NoteStretch 2 — How many cases would you need?



Keep the model and simulate the audit you wish you could run. Draw groups of 25, 50, 100 and 400 cases by resampling the test set, and record how often a true sensitivity difference of 0.10 between two groups is detectable at all. The answer tells you the minimum size of a subgroup worth reporting, and it is larger than anything on this page.








NoteStretch 3 — A threshold per group



Chapter 15 chose one threshold for everybody. Choose one per age band so that every band reaches the same sensitivity, and report what it costs in specificity and in extra referrals. Then write the paragraph you would have to put in front of a clinical governance committee to justify applying a different rule to patients of different ages.

title: 25  Exercise 9.4 — For whom is the model worst?
section: 25.12 What you can and cannot now claim
text:
25.12 What you can and cannot now claim
Can: that you can compute a model’s performance inside subgroups of a test set, report each estimate with the number of cases behind it and a bootstrap interval around it, and build a permutation noise floor that says whether a between-group gap is larger than chance produces. That is the whole machinery of a fairness audit’s measurement step, and it is not difficult.
Cannot: that this model under-serves anybody. The test set has 231 rows, the smallest band has 11 cases, and the one gap that cleared the noise floor was driven by a group with six. What you have practised is the arithmetic and the discipline of reporting it; the claim itself needs a service’s own data, a prespecified subgroup list and event counts an order of magnitude larger. An estimate reported without uncertainty is not an estimate — the same point this page makes about people rather than about variables.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
Terms as this module uses them. Where a word has a different everyday meaning, that is noted, because the gap is where misunderstanding with clinical colleagues begins.

Baseline

A deliberately unintelligent predictor — here, the mean of the training outcome — against which a model’s error is compared. A model that does not beat its baseline has not been shown to have learnt anything.

Concept shift

A change in \(P(Y \mid X)\): the same patient would now have a different outcome. Undetectable without observed outcomes.

Covariate shift

A change in \(P(X)\) with \(P(Y \mid X)\) unchanged: different patients, same rules. Detectable from inputs alone. Not automatically harmful.

Feature

A predictor, a column of X. Clinicians say “variable” and mean the same thing.

Generalisation

Performance on data not used to fit the model. In this module it always means something you measured, never something you hope for.

Held-out / test set

Rows withheld from fitting and used once, at the end, to estimate generalisation. Used twice, it stops being a test set.

Leakage

Any route by which information about the outcome, or about the test rows, reaches the model during fitting. Produces scores that are too good and cannot be reproduced.

MAE — mean absolute error

The average absolute difference between prediction and truth, in the outcome’s own units. Treats all errors in proportion to their size.

Pipeline

The ordered sequence load → define X and y → split → fit → evaluate. The order is the content: the split must precede the fit, and the evaluation must follow it.

Prediction vs inference

Prediction asks how close \(\hat{y}\) is to \(y\). Inference asks whether a relationship is real and how large it is. The same linear model serves both, which is why the same lm() call appears in Module 2 and this one with different purposes.

Training set

The rows the model is allowed to see while its parameters are estimated.

Residual

Observed minus predicted, for one row. Averaging their absolute values gives MAE; plotting them against the prediction shows whose predictions are bad.
